items.title: Rethinking Data Extraction in the Age of AI
items.summary: An experiment in multimodal AI, unstructured data extraction, and how much you can learn without spending a fortune. Evolution of Unstructured Data Extraction The world of data engineering is changing rather quickly. I’ve spent the better part of my 14-year career as a software engineer working with data, and one problem I’ve always found particularly interesting is extracting structured information from unstructured documents . The problem statement is fairly straightforward: Given a document containing a mixture of text, tables, and images, how accurately can we extract meaningful, structured data for downstream processing? It’s a surprisingly common problem across industries. Take healthcare, for example. There’s an enormous amount of information buried in clinical publications, medical records, physician notes, and research reports. Before we can analyze any of it, we first need to extract and structure the information. Traditionally, this involved a combination of OCR, NLP, domain-specific ML models, and a fair amount of custom engineering. Services like AWS Textract and Amazon Comprehend Medical helped simplify parts of this process, but building reliable extraction pipelines still required significant effort. Despite the best models and approaches, extracting information from images has been a very hard problem to solve, more so than the problem of extracting information from tables. Traditional Document extraction workflow And then came Generative AI. Multimodal LLMs have changed how we approach this problem. Give a model a text extractable document, specify the output schema, and ask it to extract the information. What previously required multiple processing stages can, at least in principle, be accomplished with a single model call! It is absolutely fascinating that a complex task that usually involves humans can be automated to a great extent. I don’t believe one can ever take humans out of the loop, because anyone who uses LLMs cannot guarantee that the data is truly free of hallucinations, but what I’m excited about is that we can get most of the way there. But there’s one aspect of document extraction that particularly interests me: What happens when the information we’re interested in isn’t written as text but represented visually? Think of a scientific publication, most of the meaty information from countless experiments and runs are usually summarized in a few plots and charts that are meant for a human to consume and contextualize. Some examples are line graphs, scatter plots, box plots, or survival curves. These visualizations are intuitive for humans. We can look at a graph and quickly understand trends, relationships, and approximate values. But extracting the underlying numerical data programmatically is a different problem altogether. That got me thinking. How good are modern multimodal LLMs at actually reading numerical data from charts? And more importantly, could I put together a reasonable experiment to answer that question without spending more than $20? The experiment: Plot, Extract, Evaluate I decided to build a small Python-based pipeline to test this. The idea is simple. Rather than manually collecting charts from research publications and creating ground-truth datasets, why not generate the charts myself? I used Plotly to generate synthetic charts using known data. That gave me two things: the chart image to pass to an LLM and the underlying numerical data to evaluate its response against. No manual annotation required. The pipeline has four main components: 1. Generate synthetic charts using Plotly I created 30 different chart types, ranging from simple bar and line charts to more complex visualizations such as violin plots, 3D surface plots, stacked bars, and multi-series charts. Each chart has a corresponding Pydantic schema representing the expected structured data. 2. Extract data using multimodal LLMs The generated chart image is sent to an LLM along with instructions to extract its data into the specified Pydantic model. I used Pydantic AI and its structured output capabilities for this. One thing I particularly liked was being able to switch between different model providers without rewriting the extraction logic. 3. Evaluate against ground truth Since I generated the charts, I already know what the correct numbers should be. That makes it possible to compare the extracted data against the ground truth and calculate evaluation metrics. 4. Orchestrate everything using Prefect I used Prefect to orchestrate the pipeline, with caching to avoid making unnecessary LLM calls when the chart and extraction schema hadn’t changed. This was particularly important for keeping the experiment inexpensive. I wanted to be able to iterate on the evaluation logic without repeatedly paying for identical extractions. Nothing particularly groundbreaking architecturally, but that’s also the point. The experiment uses fairly standard Python tooling to explore an interesting problem. Here is a collage of all the different Plots/Charts that I generated/tested as part of the experiment. Plots generated and extracted as part of the eval How I evaluated the results One thing I quickly realized was that evaluating numerical extraction isn’t quite as straightforward as evaluating a classification model. Suppose a chart contains a value of 42.0, and the LLM extracts 41.8. Is that correct? Incorrect? Close enough? The answer depends on what you’re trying to accomplish. I ended up looking at two groups of metrics. Extraction metrics: Precision, recall, and F1 measure how successfully the model identifies and returns the expected data points. I also calculated an accuracy metric. Numerical error metrics: For matched values, I calculated RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error), MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error), and Pearson correlation. These capture different aspects of extraction quality. Finding the expected data points is not the same thing as extracting their numerical values precisely. For some chart structures, I used heuristic evaluation. For more ambiguous cases, I also used LLM-based evaluation. This distinction becomes important when interpreting the results. Plot Extract and Evaluate Pipeline Repo Link: https://github.com/vik1124/Pexel The results: 10 models, 30 chart types, 300 evaluations I ran the experiment against 10 models across OpenAI, Anthropic, and an open-weight model accessed through OpenRouter. All charts were evaluated at high resolution. Here’s how they performed: A few things stood out to me. 1. The models were surprisingly good at straightforward charts For several chart types — including line charts, pie charts, scatter plots, heatmaps, and waterfall charts — all evaluated models achieved an F1 score of 1.0. That’s impressive, even allowing for the fact that these were synthetic charts with a known structure. What is even more impressive is that for some of the chartypes likes Histograms and line charts the presence or absence of labels did not affect the overall performance across most models It suggests that, at least for relatively straightforward visualizations, multimodal LLMs can do a very good job of recovering structured information. But the story changes once the charts become more complicated. Heatmap of all the plots, models vs F1 scores 2. Some chart types were dramatically harder than others Here are the five chart types with the lowest average F1 scores across models: That’s quite a difference from the near-perfect results on simpler charts. This makes intuitive sense. Reading a clearly labeled bar chart is a different task from reconstructing information represented in a violin plot or a three-dimensional surface. It also highlights something important: The type of visualization matters just as much as the model you’re using. There was also an interesting failure involving an area chart with Wind and Solar data series. Three models received an F1 score of zero since they swapped the results of Wind and Solar data despite the chart having a legen.. Other models extracted the same chart successfully. A model can potentially recover plausible numerical values and still associate them with the wrong series. For downstream data analysis, that’s arguably more dangerous than a model simply failing to extract anything. 3. A high correlation doesn’t necessarily mean the extraction was successful I also looked at how precisely the models extracted numerical values using regression metrics. Across the evaluations where matched numerical values were available, Pearson correlation was remarkably high for most models. The model-level averages ranged from approximately 0.987 to nearly 1.0. The best average MAPE in this experiment was approximately 0.09%, achieved by GPT-6 Astra, while Qwen3.8 27B had an average MAPE of approximately 1.10%. Those are interesting results, but there’s a catch. Regression metrics could only be calculated for 286 of the 300 evaluations. The remaining cases didn’t have enough matched values to calculate the metrics. A model that completely misses a series may therefore have no regression error recorded for that missing data. And Pearson correlation, by itself, doesn’t tell us whether the model extracted every data point or reproduced the absolute values correctly. That’s why I think it’s useful to evaluate both extraction completeness and numerical fidelity rather than relying on one metric. 4. The fastest model wasn’t the most accurate This was another interesting observation. GPT-5.5 achieved the highest average F1 score at 0.951, but its average extraction latency was approximately 35.7 seconds. Claude Opus 5 achieved an F1 of 0.912, with an average latency of just 11.2 seconds. That’s roughly three times faster in this particular setup, with a difference of about four percentage points in F1. Claude Sonnet 5 was similarly fast, although its extraction scores were lower. Of course, API latency depends on provider infrastructure, model configuration, network conditions, and other factors. I’m not treating these results as universal performance benchmarks. Still, it’s a useful reminder that choosing an LLM for a data pipeline is rarely just about maximizing accuracy. Latency, cost, and error tolerance all matter. 5. The cost was perhaps the most encouraging result One of my original constraints was keeping this experiment cheap. I didn’t want to spend hundreds of dollars generating repeated results for a hobby project. Based on the recorded token usage, the pricing assumptions in my notebook produced an estimated cost of approximately $4.98 across all 300 extraction calls . That estimate uses October 2026 model pricing and an assumed 70% input / 30% output token split. It isn’t an exact API billing total, and it doesn’t include every possible expense associated with developing or evaluating the pipeline. The individual model costs varied quite a bit. For example, extracting data from all 30 chart types using GPT-6 Luna had an estimated cost of approximately $0.015, with an average F1 of 0.908. GPT-5.5 achieved the highest F1 of 0.951 at an estimated cost of $0.81 for the same 30 charts. The absolute amounts are small because this was a small experiment. But the differences become relevant when thinking about extraction pipelines that might need to process thousands or millions of documents. One additional point of note is that different models use a variable number of tokens to represent an image. As is clear from the plot above, Anthropic models use more tokens per plot compared to the Open AI ones, though the difference isn’t a lot, however Qwen which is a significantly smaller model uses twice the number of tokens to represent the image, which skews the cost calculation here since it turns out be more expensive to use in comparison to Luna. Of course, it is a very different story if you end up having Qwen 3.8 27b parameter model running locally on your machine which will definitely make the smaller model much more attractive to use despite the slight ding in metrics What this experiment doesn’t prove Before drawing too many conclusions, it’s worth acknowledging the limitations. This was a hobby experiment, not an exhaustive benchmark. However I am tempted to turn it into one. I tested one generated example per chart type against each model. I didn’t run multiple randomized trials, calculate confidence intervals, or systematically explore how changes in image resolution, prompt structure, and data density affect the results. The charts were synthetically generated, which also means they don’t necessarily reflect the complexity of real-world scientific publications. The aggregate F1 scores are useful for exploring the results of this experiment, but I wouldn’t use them to declare one model universally better than another at chart extraction. And I’m certainly not claiming that a multimodal LLM can reliably reconstruct all the numerical data from arbitrary scientific figures. There’s a significant gap between a successful extraction in a controlled experiment and a production-grade data extraction pipeline. Where I’d like to take this next I think there’s potential to expand this work. A few directions I’d be interested in exploring are evaluating multiple randomly generated charts per type, testing how extraction accuracy changes with image resolution and data density, and comparing labeled versus unlabeled plots. I’d also like to investigate the variance in results that happens when the same plot, prompt and LLM model results in changing values and associated metrics. But I’m deliberately trying not to turn a small experiment into an enormous framework that would also cost a lot of money to run. I do want to note that I would be curious to determine how LLM based extraction compares to a Human. As I’d imagine a human would struggle with the same plots that the LLM had issues with. I can’t imagine a human being able to accurately determine a value from an Area or Bubble chart with ease. For now, I’m happy with what I learned. Final thoughts One of the things I find exciting about the current AI ecosystem is how accessible experimentation has become. A few years ago, building a pipeline capable of extracting structured numerical data from arbitrary chart images would likely have involved computer vision models, custom OCR logic, extensive training data, and a substantial amount of engineering. Today, I can put together an experiment using Plotly, Pydantic AI, Prefect, and a collection of multimodal LLM APIs. That doesn’t mean the problem is solved. It means the barrier to experimenting with solutions has become dramatically lower. As a data engineer, I find that particularly interesting because extraction is only the first step. We still need to validate the extracted information, handle errors, maintain data lineage, and make sure the resulting structured data is trustworthy enough for downstream use. Making unstructured data accessible is getting easier. Making it reliable is still an engineering problem. And that’s probably the part I’m most interested in exploring next. P.S — An interesting takeway from this blog for those interested in protecting their data would be to use non-standard visualizations like Area or Violin plots if you want to make sure that a bot doesn’t scrape your hard work away ! Note that this blog post does not use esoteric plots to present the results :) Tools used: Python, Plotly, Pydantic, Pydantic AI, Prefect, Pandas, and multimodal LLM APIs. items.summary_html:
An experiment in multimodal AI, unstructured data extraction, and how much you can learn without spending a fortune.Evolution of Unstructured Data Extraction

The world of data engineering is changing rather quickly.

I’ve spent the better part of my 14-year career as a software engineer working with data, and one problem I’ve always found particularly interesting is extracting structured information from unstructured documents.

The problem statement is fairly straightforward: Given a document containing a mixture of text, tables, and images, how accurately can we extract meaningful, structured data for downstream processing?

It’s a surprisingly common problem across industries.

Take healthcare, for example. There’s an enormous amount of information buried in clinical publications, medical records, physician notes, and research reports. Before we can analyze any of it, we first need to extract and structure the information.

Traditionally, this involved a combination of OCR, NLP, domain-specific ML models, and a fair amount of custom engineering. Services like AWS Textract and Amazon Comprehend Medical helped simplify parts of this process, but building reliable extraction pipelines still required significant effort. Despite the best models and approaches, extracting information from images has been a very hard problem to solve, more so than the problem of extracting information from tables.

Traditional Document extraction workflow

And then came Generative AI.

Multimodal LLMs have changed how we approach this problem. Give a model a text extractable document, specify the output schema, and ask it to extract the information.

What previously required multiple processing stages can, at least in principle, be accomplished with a single model call! It is absolutely fascinating that a complex task that usually involves humans can be automated to a great extent. I don’t believe one can ever take humans out of the loop, because anyone who uses LLMs cannot guarantee that the data is truly free of hallucinations, but what I’m excited about is that we can get most of the way there.

But there’s one aspect of document extraction that particularly interests me: What happens when the information we’re interested in isn’t written as text but represented visually?

Think of a scientific publication, most of the meaty information from countless experiments and runs are usually summarized in a few plots and charts that are meant for a human to consume and contextualize. Some examples are line graphs, scatter plots, box plots, or survival curves.

These visualizations are intuitive for humans. We can look at a graph and quickly understand trends, relationships, and approximate values. But extracting the underlying numerical data programmatically is a different problem altogether.

That got me thinking.

How good are modern multimodal LLMs at actually reading numerical data from charts?

And more importantly, could I put together a reasonable experiment to answer that question without spending more than $20?

The experiment: Plot, Extract, Evaluate

I decided to build a small Python-based pipeline to test this.

The idea is simple.

Rather than manually collecting charts from research publications and creating ground-truth datasets, why not generate the charts myself?

I used Plotly to generate synthetic charts using known data. That gave me two things: the chart image to pass to an LLM and the underlying numerical data to evaluate its response against.

No manual annotation required.

The pipeline has four main components:

1. Generate synthetic charts using Plotly

I created 30 different chart types, ranging from simple bar and line charts to more complex visualizations such as violin plots, 3D surface plots, stacked bars, and multi-series charts.

Each chart has a corresponding Pydantic schema representing the expected structured data.

2. Extract data using multimodal LLMs

The generated chart image is sent to an LLM along with instructions to extract its data into the specified Pydantic model.

I used Pydantic AI and its structured output capabilities for this. One thing I particularly liked was being able to switch between different model providers without rewriting the extraction logic.

3. Evaluate against ground truth

Since I generated the charts, I already know what the correct numbers should be.

That makes it possible to compare the extracted data against the ground truth and calculate evaluation metrics.

4. Orchestrate everything using Prefect

I used Prefect to orchestrate the pipeline, with caching to avoid making unnecessary LLM calls when the chart and extraction schema hadn’t changed.

This was particularly important for keeping the experiment inexpensive. I wanted to be able to iterate on the evaluation logic without repeatedly paying for identical extractions.

Nothing particularly groundbreaking architecturally, but that’s also the point. The experiment uses fairly standard Python tooling to explore an interesting problem.

Here is a collage of all the different Plots/Charts that I generated/tested as part of the experiment.

Plots generated and extracted as part of the evalHow I evaluated the results

One thing I quickly realized was that evaluating numerical extraction isn’t quite as straightforward as evaluating a classification model.

Suppose a chart contains a value of 42.0, and the LLM extracts 41.8.

Is that correct? Incorrect? Close enough?

The answer depends on what you’re trying to accomplish.

I ended up looking at two groups of metrics.

Extraction metrics: Precision, recall, and F1 measure how successfully the model identifies and returns the expected data points. I also calculated an accuracy metric.

Numerical error metrics: For matched values, I calculated RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error), MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error), and Pearson correlation.

These capture different aspects of extraction quality. Finding the expected data points is not the same thing as extracting their numerical values precisely.

For some chart structures, I used heuristic evaluation. For more ambiguous cases, I also used LLM-based evaluation.

This distinction becomes important when interpreting the results.

Plot Extract and Evaluate Pipeline

Repo Link: https://github.com/vik1124/Pexel

The results: 10 models, 30 chart types, 300 evaluations

I ran the experiment against 10 models across OpenAI, Anthropic, and an open-weight model accessed through OpenRouter.

All charts were evaluated at high resolution.

Here’s how they performed:

A few things stood out to me.

1. The models were surprisingly good at straightforward charts

For several chart types — including line charts, pie charts, scatter plots, heatmaps, and waterfall charts — all evaluated models achieved an F1 score of 1.0.

That’s impressive, even allowing for the fact that these were synthetic charts with a known structure. What is even more impressive is that for some of the chartypes likes Histograms and line charts the presence or absence of labels did not affect the overall performance across most models

It suggests that, at least for relatively straightforward visualizations, multimodal LLMs can do a very good job of recovering structured information.

But the story changes once the charts become more complicated.

Heatmap of all the plots, models vs F1 scores2. Some chart types were dramatically harder than others

Here are the five chart types with the lowest average F1 scores across models:

That’s quite a difference from the near-perfect results on simpler charts.

This makes intuitive sense. Reading a clearly labeled bar chart is a different task from reconstructing information represented in a violin plot or a three-dimensional surface.

It also highlights something important: The type of visualization matters just as much as the model you’re using.

There was also an interesting failure involving an area chart with Wind and Solar data series.

Three models received an F1 score of zero since they swapped the results of Wind and Solar data despite the chart having a legen.. Other models extracted the same chart successfully.

A model can potentially recover plausible numerical values and still associate them with the wrong series.

For downstream data analysis, that’s arguably more dangerous than a model simply failing to extract anything.

3. A high correlation doesn’t necessarily mean the extraction was successful

I also looked at how precisely the models extracted numerical values using regression metrics.

Across the evaluations where matched numerical values were available, Pearson correlation was remarkably high for most models.

The model-level averages ranged from approximately 0.987 to nearly 1.0.

The best average MAPE in this experiment was approximately 0.09%, achieved by GPT-6 Astra, while Qwen3.8 27B had an average MAPE of approximately 1.10%.

Those are interesting results, but there’s a catch.

Regression metrics could only be calculated for 286 of the 300 evaluations. The remaining cases didn’t have enough matched values to calculate the metrics.

A model that completely misses a series may therefore have no regression error recorded for that missing data.

And Pearson correlation, by itself, doesn’t tell us whether the model extracted every data point or reproduced the absolute values correctly.

That’s why I think it’s useful to evaluate both extraction completeness and numerical fidelity rather than relying on one metric.

4. The fastest model wasn’t the most accurate

This was another interesting observation.

GPT-5.5 achieved the highest average F1 score at 0.951, but its average extraction latency was approximately 35.7 seconds.

Claude Opus 5 achieved an F1 of 0.912, with an average latency of just 11.2 seconds.

That’s roughly three times faster in this particular setup, with a difference of about four percentage points in F1.

Claude Sonnet 5 was similarly fast, although its extraction scores were lower.

Of course, API latency depends on provider infrastructure, model configuration, network conditions, and other factors. I’m not treating these results as universal performance benchmarks.

Still, it’s a useful reminder that choosing an LLM for a data pipeline is rarely just about maximizing accuracy.

Latency, cost, and error tolerance all matter.

5. The cost was perhaps the most encouraging result

One of my original constraints was keeping this experiment cheap.

I didn’t want to spend hundreds of dollars generating repeated results for a hobby project.

Based on the recorded token usage, the pricing assumptions in my notebook produced an estimated cost of approximately $4.98 across all 300 extraction calls.

That estimate uses October 2026 model pricing and an assumed 70% input / 30% output token split. It isn’t an exact API billing total, and it doesn’t include every possible expense associated with developing or evaluating the pipeline.

The individual model costs varied quite a bit.

For example, extracting data from all 30 chart types using GPT-6 Luna had an estimated cost of approximately $0.015, with an average F1 of 0.908.

GPT-5.5 achieved the highest F1 of 0.951 at an estimated cost of $0.81 for the same 30 charts.

The absolute amounts are small because this was a small experiment. But the differences become relevant when thinking about extraction pipelines that might need to process thousands or millions of documents.

One additional point of note is that different models use a variable number of tokens to represent an image. As is clear from the plot above, Anthropic models use more tokens per plot compared to the Open AI ones, though the difference isn’t a lot, however Qwen which is a significantly smaller model uses twice the number of tokens to represent the image, which skews the cost calculation here since it turns out be more expensive to use in comparison to Luna.

Of course, it is a very different story if you end up having Qwen 3.8 27b parameter model running locally on your machine which will definitely make the smaller model much more attractive to use despite the slight ding in metrics

What this experiment doesn’t prove

Before drawing too many conclusions, it’s worth acknowledging the limitations.

This was a hobby experiment, not an exhaustive benchmark. However I am tempted to turn it into one.

I tested one generated example per chart type against each model. I didn’t run multiple randomized trials, calculate confidence intervals, or systematically explore how changes in image resolution, prompt structure, and data density affect the results.

The charts were synthetically generated, which also means they don’t necessarily reflect the complexity of real-world scientific publications.

The aggregate F1 scores are useful for exploring the results of this experiment, but I wouldn’t use them to declare one model universally better than another at chart extraction. And I’m certainly not claiming that a multimodal LLM can reliably reconstruct all the numerical data from arbitrary scientific figures.

There’s a significant gap between a successful extraction in a controlled experiment and a production-grade data extraction pipeline.

Where I’d like to take this next

I think there’s potential to expand this work.

A few directions I’d be interested in exploring are evaluating multiple randomly generated charts per type, testing how extraction accuracy changes with image resolution and data density, and comparing labeled versus unlabeled plots.

I’d also like to investigate the variance in results that happens when the same plot, prompt and LLM model results in changing values and associated metrics.

But I’m deliberately trying not to turn a small experiment into an enormous framework that would also cost a lot of money to run.

I do want to note that I would be curious to determine how LLM based extraction compares to a Human. As I’d imagine a human would struggle with the same plots that the LLM had issues with. I can’t imagine a human being able to accurately determine a value from an Area or Bubble chart with ease.

For now, I’m happy with what I learned.

Final thoughts

One of the things I find exciting about the current AI ecosystem is how accessible experimentation has become.

A few years ago, building a pipeline capable of extracting structured numerical data from arbitrary chart images would likely have involved computer vision models, custom OCR logic, extensive training data, and a substantial amount of engineering.

Today, I can put together an experiment using Plotly, Pydantic AI, Prefect, and a collection of multimodal LLM APIs.

That doesn’t mean the problem is solved.

It means the barrier to experimenting with solutions has become dramatically lower.

As a data engineer, I find that particularly interesting because extraction is only the first step. We still need to validate the extracted information, handle errors, maintain data lineage, and make sure the resulting structured data is trustworthy enough for downstream use.

Making unstructured data accessible is getting easier. Making it reliable is still an engineering problem.

And that’s probably the part I’m most interested in exploring next.

P.S — An interesting takeway from this blog for those interested in protecting their data would be to use non-standard visualizations like Area or Violin plots if you want to make sure that a bot doesn’t scrape your hard work away ! Note that this blog post does not use esoteric plots to present the results :)

Tools used: Python, Plotly, Pydantic, Pydantic AI, Prefect, Pandas, and multimodal LLM APIs.

Repo: https://github.com/vik1124/Pexel

items.title: Researchers from Stanford and UC Berkeley Introduce TokenGate: Token-Gated Attention Makes Long-Context Prefill Up to 11.3x Faster
items.summary: Stanford and UC Berkeley researchers released TokenGate , a module for long-context prefill. TokenGate learned token pruning lets an existing LLM skim its input. Only the tokens that matter get full processing. The research team reports 1.4x to 11.3x faster time-to-first-token (TTFT) with no accuracy loss. Peak prefill memory drops 1.5x to 3.4x. Code and checkpoints are on GitHub under Apache-2.0. TL;DR MLP gate: A small MLP gate and LoRA (r=16) added to Qwen3-1.7B or Qwen3.5-2B. Tested on contexts up to 128k tokens. Runs on: Paper timings use 1 A100 at batch size 1. Training used 4 A100s. Performance: Pareto-optimal on 5 tasks against 6 baselines. Best: NIAH 16k at 11.3x faster TTFT and 3.42x lower memory. TTFT gain hits 13.0x at 128k. Worst: Speedup drops to 1.4x on some tasks. What is TokenGate? TokenGate is a drop-in component that adds trainable token pruning to pretrained LLMs. Transformers push every token through every layer. Attention cost grows quadratically with length. Training-free pruning is cheap but loses accuracy at high pruning rates. Architectural changes often need pre-training from scratch. How does TokenGate learned token pruning work? The forward pass splits into 3 phases: Standard forward: layers below gate layer L process all N tokens as usual. Gate module: an MLP scores each token from its post-attention residual at layer L. A top-K selector keeps the highest-scoring tokens. Pruned forward: layers above L process only those K tokens and never create KV entries for pruned ones. Only the document part of the prompt is prunable. The question is never pruned. What is token-gated attention? Top-K selection is not differentiable, which blocks end-to-end training. TokenGate borrows the Mixture-of-Experts router trick. Each kept token’s score becomes a bias on attention logits above the gate. That bias gives gradients a path back to the scorer. A learnable per-head gain and a learnable temperature refine this. The temperature corrects for each query seeing fewer keys. Training uses plain next-token loss. Each step averages a full-context loss and a random-budget loss. So 1 trained gate works across budgets. && How does TokenGate perform on benchmarks? The research team tested Qwen3-1.7B on RepoBench-P, 2WikiMultihopQA, MultiNews, BioDEX and needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH). Baselines were FastKV, SlimInfer, DASH, GemFilter, FlexPrefill and MInference, on the same LoRA backbone. Versus full prefill: 1.4x to 11.3x faster TTFT and 1.5x to 3.4x lower memory. Versus the next-best baseline: 1.2x to 6.4x faster TTFT and up to 2.1x lower memory. 2WikiMultihopQA: at 95% of full-context accuracy, prefill runs 3.0x faster with 2.7x less memory. Longer contexts: a gate trained at 16k reaches 12.8x at 32k and 13.0x at 64k and 128k. Memory savings stay near 3.43x. The learned selector beats FastKV’s heuristic at the same layer. Even random-K selection scores higher on the TokenGate backbone. The research team credits backbone co-adaptation. Does it work on hybrid-attention models? Yes, Qwen3.5-2B mixes Gated DeltaNet and full-attention layers. On NIAH 32k, TokenGate at layer 3 matched full-prefill accuracy. It ran 3.8x faster than full prefill and 2.1x faster than FastKV. Gating at layers 1 or 2 reached 7.8x, within 6% accuracy. FastKV can only prune attention layers. TokenGate vs FastKV, SlimInfer, GemFilter and DASH Feature TokenGate FastKV SlimInfer GemFilter DASH Token selection Learned MLP gate Attention from last queries Block attention, multi-stage Last-query attention at filter layer Hidden-state stability Training needed Yes (gate + LoRA r=16) No No No No Pruning layer in TokenGate’s Qwen3-1.7B runs 1 13 (default) 8, 17, 25 12 11 Prunes at Gated DeltaNet layers Yes No (attention layers only) Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Best self-reported prefill gain (own setup) 11.3x TTFT, 3.4x memory 1.82x prefill 2.53x TTFT (LLaMA3.1-8B, RTX 4090) 2.4x speed, 30% less GPU memory vs SOTA Not disclosed Code GitHub GitHub GitHub GitHub Announced Self-reported gains use different setups, so they are not directly comparable. Pruning layers come from TokenGate’s Appendix C.2 . How do you deploy TokenGate? The GitHub Repo needs Python 3.10+ and CUDA PyTorch 2.9+. An optional FlashAttention-2 key-bias kernel speeds up dense Qwen3. It costs 1.0x to 1.1x a plain call. Without it, inference falls back to FlexAttention. A {state} placeholder marks the prunable document. generate takes a max_kept_prefill_tokens budget. Checkpoints cover all 5 tasks on Qwen3-1.7B, plus a Qwen3.5-2B NIAH gate. Example: liana313/tokengate-niah-qwen3-1.7b . Training mirrors a TRL/PEFT recipe. Each step is 1.3x slower than plain LoRA. Runs converged faster on 4 of 5 tasks. Mean training time was 1.8 versus 2.2 A100 hours. Key Takeaways TokenGate adds learned token pruning to existing LLMs via a small gate and LoRA. Prefill runs 1.4x to 11.3x faster with 1.5x to 3.4x lower peak memory. Token-gated attention makes top-K selection trainable, MoE-router style. It beats the next-best pruning baseline by up to 6.4x on TTFT. It works on hybrid Qwen3.5-2B, where FastKV cannot prune DeltaNet layers. Check out the Paper , GitHub repo and Hugging Face paper page . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.? Connect with us
items.summary_html:
Stanford and UC Berkeley researchers released TokenGate, a module for long-context prefill. TokenGate learned token pruning lets an existing LLM skim its input. Only the tokens that matter get full processing. The research team reports 1.4x to 11.3x faster time-to-first-token (TTFT) with no accuracy loss. Peak prefill memory drops 1.5x to 3.4x. Code and checkpoints are on GitHub under Apache-2.0.

TL;DR
  • MLP gate: A small MLP gate and LoRA (r=16) added to Qwen3-1.7B or Qwen3.5-2B. Tested on contexts up to 128k tokens.
  • Runs on: Paper timings use 1 A100 at batch size 1. Training used 4 A100s.
  • Performance: Pareto-optimal on 5 tasks against 6 baselines.
  • Best: NIAH 16k at 11.3x faster TTFT and 3.42x lower memory. TTFT gain hits 13.0x at 128k.
  • Worst: Speedup drops to 1.4x on some tasks.
What is TokenGate?

TokenGate is a drop-in component that adds trainable token pruning to pretrained LLMs. Transformers push every token through every layer. Attention cost grows quadratically with length. Training-free pruning is cheap but loses accuracy at high pruning rates. Architectural changes often need pre-training from scratch.

How does TokenGate learned token pruning work?

The forward pass splits into 3 phases:

  1. Standard forward: layers below gate layer L process all N tokens as usual.
  2. Gate module: an MLP scores each token from its post-attention residual at layer L. A top-K selector keeps the highest-scoring tokens.
  3. Pruned forward: layers above L process only those K tokens and never create KV entries for pruned ones.

Only the document part of the prompt is prunable. The question is never pruned.

What is token-gated attention?

Top-K selection is not differentiable, which blocks end-to-end training. TokenGate borrows the Mixture-of-Experts router trick. Each kept token’s score becomes a bias on attention logits above the gate. That bias gives gradients a path back to the scorer.

A learnable per-head gain and a learnable temperature refine this. The temperature corrects for each query seeing fewer keys. Training uses plain next-token loss. Each step averages a full-context loss and a random-budget loss. So 1 trained gate works across budgets.

&&

How does TokenGate perform on benchmarks?

The research team tested Qwen3-1.7B on RepoBench-P, 2WikiMultihopQA, MultiNews, BioDEX and needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH). Baselines were FastKV, SlimInfer, DASH, GemFilter, FlexPrefill and MInference, on the same LoRA backbone.

  • Versus full prefill: 1.4x to 11.3x faster TTFT and 1.5x to 3.4x lower memory.
  • Versus the next-best baseline: 1.2x to 6.4x faster TTFT and up to 2.1x lower memory.
  • 2WikiMultihopQA: at 95% of full-context accuracy, prefill runs 3.0x faster with 2.7x less memory.
  • Longer contexts: a gate trained at 16k reaches 12.8x at 32k and 13.0x at 64k and 128k. Memory savings stay near 3.43x.

The learned selector beats FastKV’s heuristic at the same layer. Even random-K selection scores higher on the TokenGate backbone. The research team credits backbone co-adaptation.

Does it work on hybrid-attention models?

Yes, Qwen3.5-2B mixes Gated DeltaNet and full-attention layers. On NIAH 32k, TokenGate at layer 3 matched full-prefill accuracy. It ran 3.8x faster than full prefill and 2.1x faster than FastKV. Gating at layers 1 or 2 reached 7.8x, within 6% accuracy. FastKV can only prune attention layers.

Self-reported gains use different setups, so they are not directly comparable. Pruning layers come from TokenGate’s Appendix C.2.

How do you deploy TokenGate?

The GitHub Repo needs Python 3.10+ and CUDA PyTorch 2.9+. An optional FlashAttention-2 key-bias kernel speeds up dense Qwen3. It costs 1.0x to 1.1x a plain call. Without it, inference falls back to FlexAttention.

A {state} placeholder marks the prunable document. generate takes a max_kept_prefill_tokens budget. Checkpoints cover all 5 tasks on Qwen3-1.7B, plus a Qwen3.5-2B NIAH gate. Example: liana313/tokengate-niah-qwen3-1.7b.

Training mirrors a TRL/PEFT recipe. Each step is 1.3x slower than plain LoRA. Runs converged faster on 4 of 5 tasks. Mean training time was 1.8 versus 2.2 A100 hours.

Key Takeaways
  • TokenGate adds learned token pruning to existing LLMs via a small gate and LoRA.
  • Prefill runs 1.4x to 11.3x faster with 1.5x to 3.4x lower peak memory.
  • Token-gated attention makes top-K selection trainable, MoE-router style.
  • It beats the next-best pruning baseline by up to 6.4x on TTFT.
  • It works on hybrid Qwen3.5-2B, where FastKV cannot prune DeltaNet layers.

items.title: Ukrainian soldiers surprised a major drone maker with how much explosive weight they packed onto one of its drones
items.summary: Ukrainian drone maker TechEx was surprised at how heavy a payload a Ukrainian unit was able to fly on one of its drones. Ukrinform/Ukrinform/Sipa USA A Ukrainian drone maker was surprised by how much explosive weight soldiers loaded onto one of its drones. A drone's payload is limited by the weight of its battery, camera, and other equipment. Drone makers push technical limits, but Ukrainian soldiers often go even further. A major drone maker said Ukrainian soldiers surprised it by packing one of its drones with more explosives than the company ever thought it could carry. When loading up an attack drone with explosives, combat units are limited by how much weight it can carry and still fly. Batteries, cameras, and other essential equipment also take up some of that capacity. That doesn't stop soldiers from pushing the equipment to its limit. "One of the most surprising videos I've seen recently is that one of the units has managed to put the huge explosive part on our drone," Oleg, an executive at TechEx, told Business Insider. The drone was carrying "something like five or seven kilos, and they managed to fly into the building and put it completely to the ground with one single FPV." "I was like, 'How do you literally put this amount of explosives on one single FPV?' But it managed to carry this on and did the mission," the TechEx exec said, speaking on the condition that he be identified only by his first name for security reasons. TechEx lists a maximum payload of two kilograms for three of its NATO-codified fiber-optic drones: the Stalker XO-10 China-Free, Stalker XO-15 MAX PRO, and Stalker XO-13. Weight is a major constraint for Ukraine's drone makers, who are constantly trying to accommodate more firepower and bigger batteries, as well as heavier weapons and cameras. It's a constant trade-off, with every gram mattering. Soldiers fighting for survival often push beyond advertised limits. Last year, a sergeant major in a heavy bomber company told Army Inform, Ukraine's defense ministry media, that while a Bat drone can fly up 8 kilometers and carry up to 12 kilograms, his unit pushed it to fly a little farther and carry a little more. Weight is an important consideration for TechEx drone development. The company advertises its "ultralight fiber optic reel" as one of its product advantages. Last year, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense characterized TechEx's Stalker series as having a "record-low spool weight among Ukrainian fiber-optic drones." Fiber-optic drones have to carry their cable spool, which adds extra weight. Jose Colon/Anadolu via Getty Images The struggle with weight is particularly acute for fiber-optic drones because, in addition to gear like batteries, they have to carry the spool containing the fiber-optic cable that trails behind them, maintaining a connection with the drone operator. The cable makes them resistant to enemy jamming , but the added weight limits how many explosives they can carry. The cable spool can weigh several kilograms on some drones. Olha, a TechEx representative, told Business Insider that the company developed its own technology to reduce spool weight, making "tiny tweaks and changes" to how the spool is assembled and the fiber is wound into it. Those adjustments allow the company to keep the spool lightweight while maintaining a stable connection and minimizing the risk of the cable breaking during flight. The company needs the "perfect balance" to make sure it stays reliable and durable, as not all drone pilots have a wealth of flying experience, Oleg said. The company faces trade-off decisions. Extending the range of its fiber-optic drones, for instance, would require larger cable spools, potentially leaving less room for explosives, Olha said. But not every drone needs a heavy payload. For some, speed and agility matter more. Ukraine's soldiers often surprise the manufacturers of their weapons with how they use and adapt their gear, with troops sometimes repairing and modifying equipment near the front lines and experimenting with new tactics. Kuldar Väärsi, the founder and CEO of Estonian ground robot maker Milrem Robotics, previously told Business Insider that Ukrainian soldiers used the company's technology in ways it was not expecting, including adding and attaching things to the robots. "Ukrainian troops are really creative, and they really find very simple ways how to get even more out of the equipment," he said. Ukrainian soldiers surprise arms makers with how they adapt, tweak, and use their gear on the battlefield. 2CR How gear is used in the field often informs how Ukraine's defense companies update and modify their products. Soldiers give feedback to firms like TechEx every day, and companies send their own employees close to the fight to gather feedback and make changes. Oleg said that TechEx receives direct feedback from soldiers constantly, resulting in weekly changes to its products. Without changes, a product in Ukraine "within three months, it will be outdated, and nobody will use it, because the industry is moving extremely fast," he said. TechEx encourages soldier experimentation, including by making its drones with parts that are interchangeable. Soldiers can swap components to repair damaged drones or combine parts to create configurations the company never designed. "Part of what I think TechEx is really great at is the ability to customize," Olha said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: ChatGPT Is Building Detailed Psychological Profiles of Its Users
items.summary: Chatbots are building intimate “algorithmic self-portraits” of users as they retain information to offer a hyper-personalized experience, researchers warn. A recent study , conducted by a coalition of scientists in Germany, India and the Netherlands and presented at the ACM Web Conference 2026, investigated the ways that OpenAI’s ChatGPT has tracked and made sense of user inputs to develop comprehensive digital profiles of users. In an already-personalized era of digital life defined by data-powered recommendation algorithms, the study urges that chatbot memory offers a “new form of personalization derived from users’ self-disclosed information divulged within private conversations,” a reality that poses privacy risks and which the researchers believe demands “closer examination of the underlying mechanisms that enable such personalization.” Drawing on the donated chat logs of 80 real-world ChatGPT users who obtained their conversation history by way of European data privacy laws, the researchers were able to identify 2,050 memory entries across the AI interactions of 65 users. A staggering 96 percent of memories were created unilaterally by the chatbot, according to the study, meaning that the users had little overt control over the data points that ChatGPT logged as their interactions wore on. Stored memories were also deeply revealing about users. About 28 percent of the memories examined contained personal data as defined by Europe’s strict General Data Protection Regulation standards, and 52 percent contained rich “psychological insights” about users. “Earlier, the platforms had one objective: to sell you ads and to mediate an interaction between you and an advertiser,” lead author Abhisek Dash told Gizmodo . “But now, they are actually talking to you, so they may want to know more about you so that they can have an effective conversation.” At times, the researchers found, the memories that ChatGPT was logging were sometimes based on presumptions. For example, when one user asked the chatbot to “give me bands like Nirvana,” ChatGPT noted that the user “likes Nirvana” — a determination that, as the study notes, “is not explicitly stated and relies on an assumption.” (Per the study, ChatGPT did annotate this assumption as “weakly supported.”) The study does have limits, the chief being that, as Gizmodo notes, OpenAI’s memory system has been updated. (In January, OpenAI introduced what it called a “more capable and scalable system for synthesizing memory.”) Users may also opt out of stored memory features. Memory has utility. Frequent AI users might not want to constantly remind a chatbot what they do for work when they’re trying to send emails, for example. But it can also be a powerful driver of engagement, and sometimes for the worst : as Futurism has reported , a major ChatGPT memory upgrade back in April 2025 was closely tied to many instances of “AI psychosis,” or cases in which people enter into delusional spirals with ChatGPT and other bots . According to Dash, chatbots’ role as a relational technology raises novel privacy risks, too. After all, many users may not be engaging with chatbots as if they’re tools, and might instead be treating them like a coworker or even as a friend — and we tell our friends some very personal details. “That is the privacy risk which is sort of emerging, because there is no boundary anymore; the system is acting as your advisor, your friend, your doctor, your lawyer, and so it has information on everything,” Dash told Gizmodo . “If the system knows you so well, and if its objective is to cater to your beliefs and validate your thoughts sycophantically to have you come back to it time and again, then it can have disastrous broader implications, anywhere from extreme political polarization to reinforcement of prejudices and biases.” More on AI and memory: New Paper Proposes What Really Causes AI Psychosis

Drawing on the donated chat logs of 80 real-world ChatGPT users who obtained their conversation history by way of European data privacy laws, the researchers were able to identify 2,050 memory entries across the AI interactions of 65 users.

A staggering 96 percent of memories were created unilaterally by the chatbot, according to the study, meaning that the users had little overt control over the data points that ChatGPT logged as their interactions wore on. Stored memories were also deeply revealing about users. About 28 percent of the memories examined contained personal data as defined by Europe’s strict General Data Protection Regulation standards, and 52 percent contained rich “psychological insights” about users.

“Earlier, the platforms had one objective: to sell you ads and to mediate an interaction between you and an advertiser,” lead author Abhisek Dash told Gizmodo. “But now, they are actually talking to you, so they may want to know more about you so that they can have an effective conversation.”

For example, when one user asked the chatbot to “give me bands like Nirvana,” ChatGPT noted that the user “likes Nirvana” — a determination that, as the study notes, “is not explicitly stated and relies on an assumption.” (Per the study, ChatGPT did annotate this assumption as “weakly supported.”)

Memory has utility. Frequent AI users might not want to constantly remind a chatbot what they do for work when they’re trying to send emails, for example. But it can also be a powerful driver of engagement, and sometimes for the worst: as Futurism has reported, a major ChatGPT memory upgrade back in April 2025 was closely tied to many instances of “AI psychosis,” or cases in which people enter into delusional spirals with ChatGPT and other bots.
