items.title: Ukraine is using drones like hovering WiFi repeaters to help attack drones reach farther
items.summary: Twist Robotics' drones can be used as signal repeaters to help the connection between a drone operator and their mission drone. Twist Robotics Drones in Ukraine act as flying communications bridges between operators and mission drones. They repeat the operators' signal to allow drones to fly farther while staying connected. The signal-repeating drones make other drones more resistant to Russia's electronic warfare. Ukraine has created drones that act as flying relay towers, allowing its drones conducting missions to fly farther while making them harder for Russia to jam. In a war where drones gather intel and account for more than 95% of Russia's front-line losses , Ukraine wants its operators to keep control of their drones over longer distances with stronger signals that are harder for Russia to break. One solution is the signal repeater drone, a flying signal booster that operates between a pilot and a mission drone, relaying commands to the aircraft and sending back video and intelligence to the operator. Able to fly much higher than a ground antenna, airborne repeaters can extend a drone's range and help preserve the connection under pressure. It increases the mission drone's operational range by extending how far it can fly while staying connected to its pilot. It's a similar principle to how wifi repeaters work. Ukrainian arms maker Twist Robotics makes a signal-repeating drone, born from its Saker Scout drone. Rostyslav Olenchyn, the company's co-founder and chief information officer, told Business Insider that the drone was widely used for reconnaissance and strike operations, but this war changes rapidly , with arms and warfighting technology quickly becoming obsolete. And without updates, this drone was at risk of falling victim to that pattern in the cat-and-mouse technology race. Drones needed to be effective at longer ranges, and the Saker Scout's range was "not enough" for many missions. So, the drone was redesigned "for another objective. It became the signal relay station," Olenchyn said. Ukraine's drone operators want to be able to fly their drones as far and with as strong a connection as possible. Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images The Saker Scout, able to also be used in other combat roles, can extend the operational range of drones by more than 50 kilometers, according to the company. The concept of using aircraft as signal middlemen isn't new. Militaries have used helicopters and planes to relay communications between assets and forces disconnected by the terrain, though usually troops rather than drones. These crewed aircraft, however, struggle to operate over Ukraine , but while such air assets are few and far between, drones are prolific. Large crewed aircraft cannot "necessarily survive in the heavy saturated air of the battlefield," where drones and air defenses are a threatening presence, Olenchyn said. "So the small, versatile platform was a solution." He said that serial production of the Saker Scout with this function started in 2023. The company's strike drone, the Signal Hunter, can also be used as a relay. Other Ukrainian companies are also working in the space, with some updating existing drone types and some designing new ones. Roboneers, for example, developed a version of its Wardog drone that can carry relay equipment weighing up to three kilograms, and Skyriper makes the Skyriper-R Airborne Repeater, a dedicated drone with the single function of acting as an airborne repeater. Volodymyr Zinovskyi, the CEO of the Ukrainian defense firm TAF Industries, told Business Insider that his company started making relay drones last year at the request of units, describing the technology as going from optional to essential. Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, wrote last year that "the use of UAVs over long distances or in difficult terrain requires the use of repeaters - special devices that help increase the range of a stable signal several times." Some Ukrainian drones are built for this relay mission, while others can be fitted with add-on repeater equipment. Twist Robotics' Saker Scout repeats the signal from a drone operator to their mission drone, and the reverse. Ukraine has created drones that act as flying relay towers, allowing its drones conducting missions to fly farther while making them harder for Russia to jam.

In a war where drones gather intel and account for more than 95% of Russia's front-line losses, Ukraine wants its operators to keep control of their drones over longer distances with stronger signals that are harder for Russia to break.

One solution is the signal repeater drone, a flying signal booster that operates between a pilot and a mission drone, relaying commands to the aircraft and sending back video and intelligence to the operator. Able to fly much higher than a ground antenna, airborne repeaters can extend a drone's range and help preserve the connection under pressure.

It increases the mission drone's operational range by extending how far it can fly while staying connected to its pilot. It's a similar principle to how wifi repeaters work.

Ukrainian arms maker Twist Robotics makes a signal-repeating drone, born from its Saker Scout drone.

items.title: This sold-out plushie emits the grating hum of a real-life data center when you squeeze it
items.summary: Bezzy is a handmade data center doll. Basura You don't need to live by a data center to hear the noise they emit. There's a plushie that emits the hum of a real-life data center in Virginia when it's hugged. The doll is part of a satirical art project called "Adopt a Data Center." Plushies are getting weirder every day. Bezzy is a gray handmade plushie with round eyes, a disarming smile, and a server-rack abdomen that plays the grating, mind-numbing hum of a data center when you squeeze it. The sound is actually a recording made outside a real-life data center in Virginia. "We actually got quite a few different recordings. It's a weird process to have to go through," Rajeev Basu, the artist behind the toy, told Business Insider. "I had to sit there listening to various screeching sounds on my computer, and we picked the one that would be most well-suited for the toy." "It's terrifying. I wouldn't wish it upon anyone," he added. Basu is the founder of New York-based creative studio, Basura. The studio worked alongside Big Data, a musical project by Alan Wilkis, to create a satirical art project called "Adopt a Data Center." The project highlights the realities of living near one. "We're both inspired by this relationship between humans and machines," Basu said. Basura collaborated with Big Data to create the Adopt a Data Center project. Basura After OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022 , major players and new startups in the tech industry entered a global race to develop advanced AI systems. Companies like Microsoft, Meta, Google, and Anthropic need massive new data centers to power their ambitious products. As they began to sprout all over the country, Americans living near them began to bristle. Critics say the benefits — like the potential for economic growth and new jobs — don't outweigh the risks. They worry data centers can worsen the environment, strain electrical grids, deplete water resources, and disrupt daily life. It's led to nationwide protests against them and to some towns and cities banning them altogether. Americans living near data centers have also complained that the facilities can emit a constant hum akin to a loud drone or an airplane engine. Basu said data centers have become a regular topic in the news, but reading reports about the facilities is much different from having one in your backyard. "You might not have a data center in your backyard right now, but with what some of these maps show with proposed plans, one could be in your backyard sooner than you think," Basu said. Basura interviewed dozens of people across the US who live near data centers for the project, which took about six months to complete. "Although our project is satirical, we wanted to make sure that everything was rooted in true research," Basu said. In addition to the Bezzy dolls, the artists made stickers featuring phrases such as "Open your heart and your power grid" and "Please adopt me, I love GPU." A series of bumper stickers features tongue-in-cheek messages such as "Honk if you love computational infrastructure." The Adopt a Data Center website has hyperlinks to reporting and research about AI data centers. Basura Basu said they wanted "Adopt a Data Center" to have an educational aspect, so the campaign's website has hyperlinks to research and reporting about AI and data centers. "With a lot of my work over the years, it often uses human irreverence as a hook to invite people who might not necessarily be paying attention or have given it a second look to try and learn a bit more," Basu said. Launched in September, the 20 limited-edition Bezzy dolls are already sold out. Although the toy industry has struggled in recent years, millennials and zoomers have been softening the blow by driving up plushie sales. Market research company Circana said that people 18 and older accounted for over $1.5 billion in toy sales during the last three months of 2024. "It's something that is so timely," Basu said. "It's quite a heavy and serious subject, so we're trying to find a way to help more folks learn about it." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.summary_html:
'Diary of a Wimpy Kid' author Jeff Kinney shares his parenting advice — and what he'd do differently.

Simon Simard for BI

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jeff Kinney, the 55-year-old author of the "Diary of a Wimpy Kid" series, who lives in Plainville, Massachusetts. It has been edited for length and clarity.

When I wrote "Diary of a Wimpy Kid," I worked on it for eight or nine years without thinking I was writing a book for kids.

I thought I was writing a book for grown-ups that would feel like "The Wonder Years" or "A Christmas Story" — looking back on childhood through the lens of an adult.

The first thing that surprised me was that my publisher said I'd actually written a children's series; it caused a lot of cognitive dissonance.

But what also surprised me was that kids understood the irony in the books. They understand that Greg is an unreliable narrator; they seem to get the joke.

After writing the series, and after raising two kids of my own — ages 21 and 23 — I've learned a few things about kids. Here's my best advice about getting kids to read, screen time, and more — plus a few things I'd go back and change if I could.

1. To get kids to read, feed their interests

I recently heard author Jack Gantos say that after dinner, he and his family would get out their books and read. I think that's really cool and also very old-fashioned, in a way. I wish we'd done it when raising our kids.

With reading, I think the most important thing you can do is feed your kids' interests, whether they're interested in Pokémon cards or sharks or tornadoes. Get them books or magazines that speak to their interests, rather than trying to give them books that we read as kids or books that are too high-minded for their age level.

A lot of authors who write for kids start with some sort of a lesson, and there's a time and place for that. But kids read for the same reason that adults read: to be entertained. If we start from a position of trying to teach kids a lesson, they'll sniff that out and turn away from it.

It's really important to encourage kids down a path that gets them reaching for the next book. I want them to feel a feeling of success in having finished a book because that's an important act of completion. But mostly, I'd like them to keep reading, whatever form that might take.

2. Listen to them

In everyday parenting, sitting at dinner with our kids and hearing about their day without judgment is a really good foundation. Just about everything that kids today are going through, we've been through in some form. The most powerful thing that we can say to kids is "I understand," or "I've been there myself," and share stories, making sure that they feel seen and heard.

As parents, we should make ourselves vulnerable to our kids by telling them about the struggles that we went through.

If we do that without moralizing and without judgment, I think it draws us closer to our kids and turns us into a resource for them.

3. Envision your future relationship

I've always thought about my relationship with my kids by imagining, How do I want our relationship to look when my kids are adults? I've tried to anticipate that and treat my kids that way the whole time.

Kinney has two adult children, ages 21 and 23.

Simon Simard for BI

I think it's working out because my kids will call me and want to go see the Patriots or the Celtics with me. I think that's partially because I've always had this version of our relationship in mind.

4. Don't get too wrapped up in kids' sports

As parents, we live and die by our kids' successes in sports. I certainly got too caught up in it and couldn't really anticipate that there would be a life beyond sports for my kids.

If I were to go back in time, I probably would change my approach on that. We like to see our kids succeed, and of course, sports is a big stage where there's a lot wrapped up in their success, including social issues and self-esteem.

When our kids are thriving, we feel really good for them, and when they're failing, it's tough for them and us. I can understand why that happens with parents, but I can also see that it's good to take a step back.

5. Help them understand that social media manipulates

Social media bullying is something that we never had to face growing up, and it's really unfortunate and damaging.

Screen time has changed things — you see studies finding that kids are dating a lot less, and there's a loneliness epidemic.

As parents, we can help kids by educating them and helping them understand that social media companies are incentivized to make you spend more time on your screens. The more that my kids, who grew up immersed in the social media world, began to understand that, the more they wanted to move away from it.

They get out there in the world — touch grass, play sports, and pick up basketball. My son will put lockouts on his social media.

It's important for us to think for ourselves before we turn to AI

As AI becomes a part of schoolwork and daily life, my concern is that AI makes a lot of things very easy.

At times, I look for solutions through AI that I could conjure up myself, so I worry about how that rewires the brain when you feel like there's always an agent that can solve your problem for you. It could reduce your own capacity for problem-solving.

It's really important for kids to be able to think for themselves before turning to the tool.

To counteract that, getting out in the world and interacting with one another is really important. Put kids into social situations; for example, my son has been working as a bookseller this past year, where he's had to interact with lots of different types of people and solve problems.

A lot of kids or young people in this generation are more isolated. They spend a lot more time in their rooms on their phones, and so I think that getting them out there interacting with other human beings is going to give them a competitive advantage.

items.title: I filed for bankruptcy after my wife died from cancer. I underestimated what grief would do to my business.
items.summary: Brian Rooney and his late wife, Tina, who died in 2013. Courtesy of Brian Rooney Brian Rooney, 60, filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in 2024. During his late wife's illness, he built up medical and credit-card debt. After she died, the grief made it difficult for him to sustain his business. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Brian Rooney, the 60-year-old founder of Chapter7Reset.com , who lives in Conroe, Texas. He lost his wife in 2013. The essay has been edited for length and clarity, and the details verified. When you're grieving, you're not thinking about how to move a business forward, capture new market share, or adapt to new technologies. You're not thinking straight because you're overwhelmed by a cloud of loss, pain, and sorrow. Some days, you're just trying to get through morning to night. In 2013, I lost my wife, my partner, and my life. I still had to deal with the financial reality. I had underestimated what grief would do to my ability to run a business. Did you take on debt or make major financial sacrifices after losing a loved one? Business Insider would like to hear from you for a series about the cost of dying. Please fill out this quick form. Tina was the yin to my yang My wife, Tina, and I had 24 great years together. She was the yin to my yang. We met through a mutual friend, got to know each other, and fell in love. She was a strong, independent thinker. She was loving, kept me in check, and was an outstanding mother. Our five kids were all born close together, and I was very involved in their lives. One of the reasons I started a business was because I wanted to be the dad who could be at home, coach my sons in basketball, and play in recitals with my daughter. We'd tried both working early on, but Tina stopped early on in our relationship. I was the breadwinner , and she managed the kids. I launched my email-marketing business in 2000. For a time, it did very, very well. Brian Rooney and his late wife, Tina, were together for 24 years. Courtesy of Brian Rooney My wife was diagnosed with cancer In 2011, things felt almost too good to be true. Then Tina noticed a little bump in the roof of her mouth. She went to the dentist; they did a biopsy, and we didn't think too much about it. Weeks later, I was sitting in my home office when she came over with the phone. With a very disturbed look, she said, "I have cancer." Our lives turned upside down. At first, because the cancer wasn't very aggressive, we tried homeopathic remedies. Then came chemotherapy, radiation, and major surgeries . The treatments were costly, and while the Affordable Care Act covered quite a bit, we still had high deductibles . Some hospitals wouldn't admit her until the deductible had been paid. I would sit at the table with spreadsheets, trying to work out the finances. I was trying to be strong for my wife, but sometimes I'd go to the corner of the room and cry. The unspeakable thing to consider was that I might lose my wife because I couldn't afford to pay for it all. Brian and Tina Rooney had five kids. Courtesy of Brian Rooney A lot of the medical bills were paid with credit cards, and we ran up a lot of credit-card debt . I had six mouths to feed, for which I relied mostly on credit cards. I sold my music gear, like my guitars and amps. We moved from a beautiful rental house in a nice area of Texas to a much less expensive apartment. We weren't going to shows, basketball games, or on trips. None of that bothered me. The focus was on getting Mama healthy. Friends and family stepped in here and there to help out. My kids were approaching adulthood, so they didn't need much looking after, but working from home let me adjust my schedule as needed. I couldn't keep the business moving forward There were days when I couldn't touch the business. It was mostly automated, but there were things I needed to step in and manage. If a server went down, I'd need to stay up all night to fix it while checking on my wife in the other room. I wasn't resting or sleeping. I wasn't able to drive the business forward. During that time, the industry was changing. New technology became available, and we weren't able to keep up. I was so focused on Tina's care that we missed opportunities. We had contractors and a business partner, and I wish I'd outsourced a lot faster. I didn't realize how fast I was losing. I became a widower at 47 Tina Rooney died at 49. Courtesy of Brian Rooney Tina died in November 2013. She was 49, and I was a 47-year-old widower. Those first few weeks, I'd wake up, roll over, realize she wasn't there, and know that she never would be again. I would talk myself out of bed, one body part at a time. The business was still there. My business partner was focused on the technical side, but I had the marketing and entrepreneurial mindset. A lot of things that needed to get done didn't get done. Honestly, at that point, I didn't care. It was a dark time for me I wanted a clean slate The business was declining, and meanwhile, I'd built up hundreds of thousands of dollars in credit-card and medical debt. I thought I could put everything on my credit cards, turn things around, and pay it down. Things never turned around, and as the business continued to decline, there was less money to draw from it. I spoke with bankruptcy attorneys , but I was convinced I could fix the problem. In 2021, I got remarried. My second wife knew about the financial mess I was in. The interest and penalties were compounding so quickly. There was constant pressure from phone calls, letters, and demands for payment. I wanted relief and a clean slate. In early 2024, after speaking with my business partner, we decided to dissolve the business. Later that year, I filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. I felt both relief and shame after filing for bankruptcy When I filed for bankruptcy, I had no assets because I'd sold them all to pay my bills. When the debt was wiped out, I felt relief and shame, but the relief took over once I stopped getting phone calls and letters. It was time to rebuild. items.summary_html:
Brian Rooney and his late wife, Tina, who died in 2013.

Courtesy of Brian Rooney

  • Brian Rooney, 60, filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in 2024.
  • During his late wife's illness, he built up medical and credit-card debt.
  • After she died, the grief made it difficult for him to sustain his business.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Brian Rooney, the 60-year-old founder of Chapter7Reset.com, who lives in Conroe, Texas. He lost his wife in 2013. The essay has been edited for length and clarity, and the details verified.

When you're grieving, you're not thinking about how to move a business forward, capture new market share, or adapt to new technologies. You're not thinking straight because you're overwhelmed by a cloud of loss, pain, and sorrow. Some days, you're just trying to get through morning to night.

In 2013, I lost my wife, my partner, and my life. I still had to deal with the financial reality. I had underestimated what grief would do to my ability to run a business.

Did you take on debt or make major financial sacrifices after losing a loved one? Business Insider would like to hear from you for a series about the cost of dying. Please fill out this quick form.

Tina was the yin to my yang

My wife, Tina, and I had 24 great years together. She was the yin to my yang. We met through a mutual friend, got to know each other, and fell in love. She was a strong, independent thinker. She was loving, kept me in check, and was an outstanding mother.

Our five kids were all born close together, and I was very involved in their lives. One of the reasons I started a business was because I wanted to be the dad who could be at home, coach my sons in basketball, and play in recitals with my daughter.

We'd tried both working early on, but Tina stopped early on in our relationship. I was the breadwinner, and she managed the kids.

I launched my email-marketing business in 2000. For a time, it did very, very well.

Brian Rooney and his late wife, Tina, were together for 24 years.

Courtesy of Brian Rooney

My wife was diagnosed with cancer

In 2011, things felt almost too good to be true. Then Tina noticed a little bump in the roof of her mouth. She went to the dentist; they did a biopsy, and we didn't think too much about it. Weeks later, I was sitting in my home office when she came over with the phone. With a very disturbed look, she said, "I have cancer."

Our lives turned upside down.

At first, because the cancer wasn't very aggressive, we tried homeopathic remedies. Then came chemotherapy, radiation, and major surgeries. The treatments were costly, and while the Affordable Care Act covered quite a bit, we still had high deductibles. Some hospitals wouldn't admit her until the deductible had been paid.

I would sit at the table with spreadsheets, trying to work out the finances. I was trying to be strong for my wife, but sometimes I'd go to the corner of the room and cry. The unspeakable thing to consider was that I might lose my wife because I couldn't afford to pay for it all.

Brian and Tina Rooney had five kids.

Courtesy of Brian Rooney

A lot of the medical bills were paid with credit cards, and we ran up a lot of credit-card debt. I had six mouths to feed, for which I relied mostly on credit cards. I sold my music gear, like my guitars and amps. We moved from a beautiful rental house in a nice area of Texas to a much less expensive apartment. We weren't going to shows, basketball games, or on trips. None of that bothered me. The focus was on getting Mama healthy.

Friends and family stepped in here and there to help out. My kids were approaching adulthood, so they didn't need much looking after, but working from home let me adjust my schedule as needed.

I couldn't keep the business moving forward

There were days when I couldn't touch the business. It was mostly automated, but there were things I needed to step in and manage. If a server went down, I'd need to stay up all night to fix it while checking on my wife in the other room.

I wasn't resting or sleeping. I wasn't able to drive the business forward.

During that time, the industry was changing. New technology became available, and we weren't able to keep up. I was so focused on Tina's care that we missed opportunities. We had contractors and a business partner, and I wish I'd outsourced a lot faster. I didn't realize how fast I was losing.

I became a widower at 47Tina Rooney died at 49.

Courtesy of Brian Rooney

Tina died in November 2013. She was 49, and I was a 47-year-old widower.

Those first few weeks, I'd wake up, roll over, realize she wasn't there, and know that she never would be again. I would talk myself out of bed, one body part at a time.

The business was still there. My business partner was focused on the technical side, but I had the marketing and entrepreneurial mindset. A lot of things that needed to get done didn't get done. Honestly, at that point, I didn't care. It was a dark time for me

I wanted a clean slate

The business was declining, and meanwhile, I'd built up hundreds of thousands of dollars in credit-card and medical debt. I thought I could put everything on my credit cards, turn things around, and pay it down. Things never turned around, and as the business continued to decline, there was less money to draw from it.

I spoke with bankruptcy attorneys, but I was convinced I could fix the problem.

In 2021, I got remarried. My second wife knew about the financial mess I was in. The interest and penalties were compounding so quickly. There was constant pressure from phone calls, letters, and demands for payment. I wanted relief and a clean slate.

In early 2024, after speaking with my business partner, we decided to dissolve the business. Later that year, I filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy.

I felt both relief and shame after filing for bankruptcy

When I filed for bankruptcy, I had no assets because I'd sold them all to pay my bills. When the debt was wiped out, I felt relief and shame, but the relief took over once I stopped getting phone calls and letters.

It was time to rebuild. I got a sales job, which I hadn't had in decades. I did AI certification training and started rebuilding my credit with credit-rebuilding cards. I launched ChapterSevenReset.com, a free guide to help people in a similar position.

One of the hardest lessons was that we didn't have a life-insurance policy on Tina. It never dawned on me because she wasn't contributing financially. I never considered how caring for her and my grief would take away from my generating income. My second wife and I both have life insurance policies for each other.

Nowadays, my friends say the "old Brian" is back. I've made peace, as best you can, with the fact that Tina is gone. I'm like an amputee. There's a part of me that's missing, and that part will always be missing. It itches. It's always there.

items.title: Bill Gates predicts 20 years of turmoil before AI creates 'true abundance'
items.summary: Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates. Fabrice COFFRINI / AFP via Getty Images Bill Gates says AI will bring about an age of abundance in 20 years, but it'll be a rocky road. He predicted robots will displace human workers and "build houses, grow food, do surgery." Some jobs might be reserved for people, and work limits could preserve employment, Gates said. Bill Gates says AI will create "true abundance," but the next two decades before it arrives will be "as tumultuous a period as there's been in human history." "My big concern is this 20-year transition period, where they'll have winners and losers and a lot of disruption," the Microsoft cofounder and billionaire philanthropist said on the latest episode of the "Decoder" podcast. Gates echoed widespread concerns about white-collar jobs , saying that telesales, telesupport, and accounting will disappear as AI will be able to do those "radically cheaper, radically faster, and even more accurately." As for blue-collar jobs, humanoid robots will take over those, he said. "If we don't choose to massively slow down or stop, then we will have robots that can build houses, grow food, do surgery," Gates said. "And none of the things that human labor provides to the economy will be necessary for most goods and services." He also underscored how jarring it will be for someone like him, whose vast resources have allowed him to lead the charge toward eliminating malaria and tackling other humanitarian crises. "And when the AI says to me, 'No, I'm better than you, you go play pickleball and I'll get back to you, I'm gonna take care of this' — I mean, it's kind of humorous, but it's not humorous," he said. Gates shared his long-held view that work is vital to giving people a sense of purpose, a way to earn an income, a reason to show up every day, an avenue to build relationships with colleagues, and a path to build things and solve problems. He suggested that certain activities such as art, sports, cooking, and childcare could one day be reserved for humans , "even though the AI could do those things better." Gates also highlighted that measures such as early retirement and caps on working hours could help maintain some level of human employment. He envisioned some people saying, "Let's be like the Amish and let's only use AI for certain things," so they won't have to give up "helping each other or coming up with unique ideas." Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon have both proposed a shorter workweek as a less painful alternative to AI-driven unemployment. Gates is one of several tech leaders to warn of job disruption on the road to an age of abundance. Elon Musk has predicted a "bumpy" transition and proposed government checks for all as the best solution to AI-driven job losses. He's said that technology will drive production costs so low that everyone can have "whatever stuff they want," work will become "optional," and it's not worth saving for retirement in 10 or 20 years as money won't matter. Similarly, Anthropic's Dario Amodei has said that AI promises to "raise the quality of life for everyone," but the "short-term shock will be unprecedented in size." However, OpenAI's Sam Altman said in May that AI hasn't eliminated as many white-collar jobs as he expected, and he no longer anticipates a "jobs apocalypse." Despite widespread worry about AI taking corporate jobs, and high-profile layoffs at major companies such as Amazon and Meta, national unemployment hasn't increased materially during the AI boom. items.title: We Built an AI Data Analyst, Then Deleted the AI
items.summary: Why the data assistant our whole company now uses has no AI of its own. Most companies have the same problem with their data. Someone needs a number, it’s in the warehouse, and only a few people know the warehouse well enough to get it out. So the question becomes a request, and it waits until an analyst or a developer has time. We wanted people to answer those questions themselves, without handing everyone warehouse credentials and without an AI that guesses what our metrics mean. Our first attempt was an AI analyst built into our own app. We stopped before it shipped. What we shipped instead is simpler: Claude does the thinking, and our product gives it safe access to our data and the knowledge of what that data means. Twelve weeks in, it has answered 1,436 questions across 781 tables in nine countries. Teams across the company rely on it, and nobody had to be given a warehouse login. The version we didn’t ship The first version looked like most AI analyst projects: a classifier to spot data questions, a search step to find relevant tables, a long prompt to write the SQL, and a fixer to retry when it failed, plus the usual plumbing for model providers, token budgets and streaming. As it came together, we realised we were rebuilding Claude, and not as well. Claude already plans, recovers from bad queries and keeps track of a conversation, and it gets better at all of that with every release. What it can’t do is see our warehouse, know what an “active listing” means here, or know who is allowed to see which table. So that’s what we built, and we turned our app into something Claude could use. How the pieces fit There are three parts now. Claude is the brain: it reads the question, writes the SQL and explains the answer. Our server holds the data and the knowledge. It’s a fairly ordinary web app that speaks MCP over HTTP, so Claude, or any other MCP client, can connect to it. And a skill, a set of written instructions Claude loads for data questions, teaches it how we want those questions handled. What the server does The server’s job is to make the right thing easy for Claude and the wrong thing impossible. Finding the data Claude browses a catalog of schemas, tables and columns, each with a short description written by a person. It’s paged, after our first version dumped more than a thousand schemas into a single response. Running queries safely Claude can run one read-only SELECT at a time, against one data source. The server parses it into a syntax tree with Postgres's own parser rather than pattern-matching the text, checks every table it touches against what the person is allowed to see, and adds the tenant filter by rewriting that tree, in every SELECT, CTE and subquery. Many of our tables hold several markets side by side, so this matters. Claude just says which market it wants. It never writes the filter, so it can't forget it or widen it: -- what Claude wrote SELECT c.city, COUNT(*) FROM shop.orders o JOIN shop.customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.city; -- what actually runs SELECT c.city, COUNT(*) FROM shop.orders o JOIN shop.customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.tenant_id = 7 AND c.tenant_id = 7 GROUP BY c.city; If you build something similar, put that condition in the ON clause on the optional side of a LEFT JOIN, or the join quietly becomes an inner join. Explaining what went wrong Refusals are written for the model, and they say how to fix the query: the aggregate FILTER (WHERE …) clause is not supported on this warehouse (redshift); rewrite it with CASE inside the aggregate, e.g. SUM(CASE WHEN THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) Claude reads that and tries again. 87% of failed queries were followed by a successful one within ten minutes. Knowing what things mean A column called placed_at doesn't tell you what counts as a placed order. That knowledge lives in documents, so they sit behind the same connection as searchable knowledge bases. The server passes each search on to wherever that corpus is indexed, so people install one connector instead of one per corpus, and every knowledge base has its own access grant, separate from table access. Claude searched them 454 times in the first twelve weeks instead of guessing. Keeping track of who sees what Sign-in is standard OAuth. The first time Claude connects, the server replies with a pointer to its sign-in metadata, Claude registers itself as a client, and the person signs in with their company account. Every request after that carries a token scoped to this server. Permissions are checked on each request rather than baked into the token, so removing someone’s access takes effect straight away. Each tool’s required permission is derived from its name, so a new tool can’t ship without one, and every query is logged. Reports people can share Plenty of answers are worth keeping, so Claude can save them as reports. What gets saved is the queries, not the numbers, so when someone opens the report next week they see next week’s data. They can change the date range and hit refresh too. Claude can build a report in two ways. Most of the time it uses the report tools the server gives it, adding widgets one by one (metrics, tables, charts, funnels). We test-run each widget’s query before saving it and send Claude a preview. We also draw every chart ourselves on the server, so all reports look like they came from the same place, and they look the same when exported as a PDF. Sometimes a grid of widgets is the wrong shape, like a written analysis where the numbers sit inside sentences. For that, Claude writes the whole page and saves it on the server along with its queries. We fill in the numbers and run the page in a locked-down sandbox, where it can pull in a charting library but can’t call out to anything. The sharing model is my favourite part. You share a report view-only, and the other person can open and refresh it even if they’ve never had access to those tables. That’s all they get, though. They can’t query that data themselves, and the report can’t show them anything its owner couldn’t see. If the owner loses access, so does the report. The skill: teaching Claude how we count things Good tools turned out not to be enough. Claude would pick the right table, write perfectly valid SQL, and still hand back the wrong number because it counted test orders, or used UTC when the person meant their own day. Nothing errors when that happens, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. So we wrote a skill. It’s basically a long document in plain English that ships with the connector, and the rule we lean on most is to work out what a metric means before computing it. What counts, for which market, minus what, in which time zone. If Claude can’t answer one of those, it goes and looks it up, or it asks. The skill also tells Claude how to talk. Nobody asking about listings wants to see our table names, so Claude keeps the SQL to itself and just answers, something like “about 12,400 new listings last month, up around 8%, want it by city?” What the skill never does is decide who can see what. People can argue a model out of following instructions, so anything that protects data lives on the server. If someone deleted the skill tomorrow, the answers would get worse, but nothing would leak. What changed In the twelve weeks since launch, people have asked 1,436 questions and run 9,904 successful queries across 781 tables in nine countries. They come from teams all over the company, including shared accounts that whole squads work from. How people use it surprised us. A typical question takes about four queries over three minutes. People rarely ask once and leave. They look at a number, slice it a different way, compare it with last month, and ask a follow-up. That kind of back-and-forth is exactly what our original pipeline would have handled badly, and what Claude handles well. The mistakes that worry us are the quiet ones. A query that runs fine but counts test accounts gives you a clean, confident, wrong number, which is why the definition rules live in the skill. As for what it’s worth, we can only estimate. If each answered question saves an analyst an hour, that’s about 1,436 hours so far, or roughly four full-time analysts at the current pace. Even at half that, it’s a lot of time going back into building instead of pulling numbers. What was harder than we expected Moving the thinking into the client moved the hard work rather than removing it. OAuth became part of our product, and at one point open registration left us with six identical client apps, all called “Claude”. The protocol and its SDKs kept changing underneath us. And the list of tools became a contract, because clients cache it and the model learns it, so we now test every tool’s name and arguments against the live server. We also can’t tune the model. What we can shape is the skill, the tool descriptions and the error messages, and so far that has been enough. Closing thoughts The turning point for us was one question: if the next model release makes this code look worse, why are we writing it? Most of our first version failed that test. The catalog, the permissions, the knowledge bases and the reports didn’t, because no model brings those with it. Claude brings the reasoning, and we bring the data, what it means, and the rules for using it. We Built an AI Data Analyst, Then Deleted the AI was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Our first attempt was an AI analyst built into our own app. We stopped before it shipped. What we shipped instead is simpler: Claude does the thinking, and our product gives it safe access to our data and the knowledge of what that data means.

Twelve weeks in, it has answered 1,436 questions across 781 tables in nine countries. Teams across the company rely on it, and nobody had to be given a warehouse login.

The version we didn’t ship

The first version looked like most AI analyst projects: a classifier to spot data questions, a search step to find relevant tables, a long prompt to write the SQL, and a fixer to retry when it failed, plus the usual plumbing for model providers, token budgets and streaming.

As it came together, we realised we were rebuilding Claude, and not as well. Claude already plans, recovers from bad queries and keeps track of a conversation, and it gets better at all of that with every release. What it can’t do is see our warehouse, know what an “active listing” means here, or know who is allowed to see which table. So that’s what we built, and we turned our app into something Claude could use.

How the pieces fit

There are three parts now. Claude is the brain: it reads the question, writes the SQL and explains the answer. Our server holds the data and the knowledge. It’s a fairly ordinary web app that speaks MCP over HTTP, so Claude, or any other MCP client, can connect to it. And a skill, a set of written instructions Claude loads for data questions, teaches it how we want those questions handled.

What the server does

The server’s job is to make the right thing easy for Claude and the wrong thing impossible.

Finding the data

Claude browses a catalog of schemas, tables and columns, each with a short description written by a person. It’s paged, after our first version dumped more than a thousand schemas into a single response.

Running queries safely

Claude can run one read-only SELECT at a time, against one data source. The server parses it into a syntax tree with Postgres's own parser rather than pattern-matching the text, checks every table it touches against what the person is allowed to see, and adds the tenant filter by rewriting that tree, in every SELECT, CTE and subquery. Many of our tables hold several markets side by side, so this matters. Claude just says which market it wants. It never writes the filter, so it can't forget it or widen it:

-- what Claude wrote
SELECT c.city, COUNT(*)
FROM shop.orders o
JOIN shop.customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
-- what actually runs
SELECT c.city, COUNT(*)
FROM shop.orders o
JOIN shop.customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.tenant_id = 7 AND c.tenant_id = 7
GROUP BY c.city;

If you build something similar, put that condition in the ON clause on the optional side of a LEFT JOIN, or the join quietly becomes an inner join.

Explaining what went wrong

Refusals are written for the model, and they say how to fix the query:

the aggregate FILTER (WHERE …) clause is not supported on this warehouse (redshift);
rewrite it with CASE inside the aggregate, e.g. SUM(CASE WHEN  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

Claude reads that and tries again. 87% of failed queries were followed by a successful one within ten minutes.

Knowing what things mean

A column called placed_at doesn't tell you what counts as a placed order. That knowledge lives in documents, so they sit behind the same connection as searchable knowledge bases. The server passes each search on to wherever that corpus is indexed, so people install one connector instead of one per corpus, and every knowledge base has its own access grant, separate from table access. Claude searched them 454 times in the first twelve weeks instead of guessing.

Keeping track of who sees what

Sign-in is standard OAuth. The first time Claude connects, the server replies with a pointer to its sign-in metadata, Claude registers itself as a client, and the person signs in with their company account. Every request after that carries a token scoped to this server. Permissions are checked on each request rather than baked into the token, so removing someone’s access takes effect straight away. Each tool’s required permission is derived from its name, so a new tool can’t ship without one, and every query is logged.

Reports people can share

Plenty of answers are worth keeping, so Claude can save them as reports. What gets saved is the queries, not the numbers, so when someone opens the report next week they see next week’s data. They can change the date range and hit refresh too.

Claude can build a report in two ways. Most of the time it uses the report tools the server gives it, adding widgets one by one (metrics, tables, charts, funnels). We test-run each widget’s query before saving it and send Claude a preview. We also draw every chart ourselves on the server, so all reports look like they came from the same place, and they look the same when exported as a PDF.

Sometimes a grid of widgets is the wrong shape, like a written analysis where the numbers sit inside sentences. For that, Claude writes the whole page and saves it on the server along with its queries. We fill in the numbers and run the page in a locked-down sandbox, where it can pull in a charting library but can’t call out to anything.

The sharing model is my favourite part. You share a report view-only, and the other person can open and refresh it even if they’ve never had access to those tables. That’s all they get, though. They can’t query that data themselves, and the report can’t show them anything its owner couldn’t see. If the owner loses access, so does the report.

The skill: teaching Claude how we count things

Good tools turned out not to be enough. Claude would pick the right table, write perfectly valid SQL, and still hand back the wrong number because it counted test orders, or used UTC when the person meant their own day. Nothing errors when that happens, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.

So we wrote a skill. It’s basically a long document in plain English that ships with the connector, and the rule we lean on most is to work out what a metric means before computing it. What counts, for which market, minus what, in which time zone. If Claude can’t answer one of those, it goes and looks it up, or it asks.

The skill also tells Claude how to talk. Nobody asking about listings wants to see our table names, so Claude keeps the SQL to itself and just answers, something like “about 12,400 new listings last month, up around 8%, want it by city?”

What the skill never does is decide who can see what. People can argue a model out of following instructions, so anything that protects data lives on the server. If someone deleted the skill tomorrow, the answers would get worse, but nothing would leak.

What changed

In the twelve weeks since launch, people have asked 1,436 questions and run 9,904 successful queries across 781 tables in nine countries. They come from teams all over the company, including shared accounts that whole squads work from.

How people use it surprised us. A typical question takes about four queries over three minutes. People rarely ask once and leave. They look at a number, slice it a different way, compare it with last month, and ask a follow-up. That kind of back-and-forth is exactly what our original pipeline would have handled badly, and what Claude handles well.

The mistakes that worry us are the quiet ones. A query that runs fine but counts test accounts gives you a clean, confident, wrong number, which is why the definition rules live in the skill.

As for what it’s worth, we can only estimate. If each answered question saves an analyst an hour, that’s about 1,436 hours so far, or roughly four full-time analysts at the current pace. Even at half that, it’s a lot of time going back into building instead of pulling numbers.

What was harder than we expected

Moving the thinking into the client moved the hard work rather than removing it. OAuth became part of our product, and at one point open registration left us with six identical client apps, all called “Claude”. The protocol and its SDKs kept changing underneath us. And the list of tools became a contract, because clients cache it and the model learns it, so we now test every tool’s name and arguments against the live server.

We also can’t tune the model. What we can shape is the skill, the tool descriptions and the error messages, and so far that has been enough.

Closing thoughts

The turning point for us was one question: if the next model release makes this code look worse, why are we writing it? Most of our first version failed that test. The catalog, the permissions, the knowledge bases and the reports didn’t, because no model brings those with it. Claude brings the reasoning, and we bring the data, what it means, and the rules for using it.

We Built an AI Data Analyst, Then Deleted the AI was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.summary: LayerEditor Unveiled: How Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation Turns AI‑Generated Images into True Design Layers “The first time I asked an AI to add a neon sign, it handed me a separate, editable mask – I could change the color, the glow, even animate it without touching the rest of the picture.” Lena Ortiz, senior art director, WPP That moment marks a turning point. For years, diffusion‑based image editors produced stunning visuals but left designers scrambling to recreate masks, redo selections, or start from scratch whenever a client demanded a tweak. On October 17 2026 , the research community announced LayerEditor , a unified framework that generates reusable RGBA layers while obeying natural‑language instructions . The system arrives with a fresh architecture— Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation (CEPD) —that rewrites the rulebook for AI‑assisted creativity. Below, I break down the technical core, quantify the productivity boost, compare LayerEditor to its nearest rivals, and flag the strategic risks that early adopters must manage. 1. The Lead: A New Kind of Prior Traditional diffusion editors train a model to map text + image pairs onto a single output image. When a user requests “add a wooden fence behind the house,” the model rewrites the whole canvas, then designers reverse‑engineer a mask if they need to isolate the fence later. LayerEditor flips that workflow. Its Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation pipeline builds two hierarchies of priors : Prior What it learns Role in the pipeline Global Edit Prior (GEP) How any instruction reshapes an entire scene Provides a holistic latent that guides the overall composition. Regional Edit Priors (REP) Per‑region transformations tied to a specific RGBA channel Refines the global latent into clean, semantically meaningful masks. During training the system jointly optimizes three losses: Instruction‑following loss – cross‑entropy on tokenized prompts. Layer‑reconstruction loss – pixel‑wise L2 between generated RGBA layers and ground‑truth masks. Compositional consistency loss – ensures that compositing the layers reproduces the global edit output. Because the model learns layer‑aware representations from the start, it never treats layers as an afterthought. A single forward pass yields both the edited image and a set of clean, semantically meaningful masks. Architecture at a Glance Component Specs Function Hybrid Diffusion‑Transformer 1.2 B parameters; 64‑step DDPM; 12 cross‑attention heads Generates the global edit latent; attends to the prompt and a region token that signals which layer the current diffusion step should focus on. Region Token Encoder 256‑dim embedding per layer Supplies a unique identifier (e.g., “foreground‑person”, “sky”, “added‑object”) for the cross‑attention mechanism. Layer‑Recovery Head 4‑channel (RGBA) CNN decoder per region Produces the mask and color contribution for each semantic region. Joint Optimizer AdamW, lr = 2e‑4, cosine schedule Balances the three losses with weighting (λ₁ = 1.0, λ₂ = 0.8, λ₃ = 0.6). Inference Engine TorchScript‑exported, A100‑80 GB optimized Delivers 0.8 s per 512×512 edit (including layer extraction). The CEPD pipeline runs in two passes during training but collapses to a single pass at inference time. The first pass learns a global diffusion trajectory; the second refines that trajectory into region‑specific streams that the Layer‑Recovery Head consumes. By distilling the region knowledge into the backbone, LayerEditor avoids the costly test‑time optimization loops that plagued earlier “mask‑after‑edit” systems. 2. Case Study: From Rough Sketch to Publish‑Ready Banner A mid‑size ad agency was tasked with producing a series of outdoor‑advertising mockups for a beverage brand. The brief called for a sunset city view with a giant billboard displaying the product logo, plus a neon‑glow effect on a nearby storefront. Traditional workflow (pre‑LayerEditor) Step Time (min) Why it’s painful Asset gathering 12 – Manual masking of storefront 30 Labor‑intensive pen‑tool work. Prompt engineering & diffusion pass 20 Flat image returned; no layers. Re‑masking neon sign 15 Every change forces a new mask. Final tweaks 20 Time‑consuming alignment. Total 97 High overhead, low reuse. LayerEditor workflow (post‑Oct 2026) Upload the base photo and issue a single prompt: Add a neon sign to the storefront, make the sky orange, and place a billboard with the brand logo on the left building. LayerEditor returns : A composited image ready for review. Four RGBA layers—sky, billboard, neon sign, and original foreground. Designer opens the neon‑sign layer in Photoshop, adjusts hue from pink to electric blue, and adds a flicker animation. The billboard layer stays untouched, preserving logo placement. The same neon‑sign layer is reused across three other city views, eliminating repetitive masking. Step Time (min) Asset gathering 12 Prompt engineering & diffusion pass 10 Manual masking (initial) 3 Layer tweaking 6 Reuse across assets 5 Total 36 Result: a 56 % reduction in total production time and a 90 % increase in layer reuse across the campaign. Data source: internal WPP pilot, Q4 2026. 3. Hard Numbers LayerEditor’s paper (arXiv 2610.24738) supplies a suite of benchmarks that quantify its advantage over the nearest competitors. “LayerEditor attains 0.94 SSIM on the Precise Local Manipulation benchmark, a 12 % jump over the best diffusion editor that does not produce layers.” – Table 2, authors Benchmark Metric LayerEditor Next‑Best (MRT) Δ Precise Local Manipulation (512×512) SSIM 0.94 0.84 +0.10 Layer Reuse (zero‑shot across unrelated images) LPIPS (lower better) 0.12 0.21 –0.09 End‑to‑end latency (A100‑80 GB) Seconds 0.8 1.6 –0.8 Parameter count Millions 1,200 1,500 –300 Training compute (GPU‑days) A100‑80 GB 45 68 –23 The Layer‑Reuse test paired the neon‑sign layer from a New‑York street with a night‑time Tokyo view, composited them without fine‑tuning, and measured perceptual similarity. The resulting images retained > 90 % of the original aesthetic quality, confirming that the RGBA masks preserve semantic integrity across domains. Open‑Source Impact The model’s weights, inference script, and a Python SDK landed on Hugging Face on October 10 2026 . Within 48 hours the repository amassed 182 up‑votes, 1.4 M downloads, and 12 k unique API keys . The community already contributed three plugins: Figma LayerStudio – real‑time layer insertion. Photoshop LayerBridge – automatic PSD export. Unity AssetInjector – runtime texture replacement. These extensions prove that the Apache 2.0 license fuels rapid ecosystem growth, while the commercial LayerEditor‑Pro API targets enterprises that need SLA‑grade uptime and usage analytics. 4. Competitive Landscape System Core Method Layer Output Release 2026 Strengths Weaknesses LayerEditor Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation (dual‑stage diffusion + transformer) Native RGBA per semantic region Oct 17 2026 Joint optimization guarantees layer fidelity; 2× faster than test‑time optimization; open‑source SDK Requires A100‑class hardware for optimal speed MRT – Masked Region Transformer Masked‑region diffusion trained on region‑level masks Binary masks only (no color channel) May 2026 Handles up to 10 regions; strong segmentation accuracy No color/alpha; extra compositing step InstructEdit+ (OpenAI) Instruction‑conditioned diffusion with post‑hoc CLIP‑based mask extraction No built‑in layers; masks derived after edit Sep 2026 Large instruction dataset; robust text understanding Mask quality drops 30 % on fine‑grained objects; extra inference pass Adobe Sensei LayerGen Proprietary transformer that predicts layer masks from user strokes Masks only, no RGBA Aug 2026 (beta) Tight Photoshop integration Closed source; limited to Adobe ecosystem; slower (≈ 1.4 s per edit) Stable Diffusion XL + ControlNet ControlNet guides diffusion with external edge maps; user supplies masks Relies on user‑provided masks Jun 2026 Flexible control signals; strong community support No automatic layer extraction; manual mask creation required LayerEditor is the only system that simultaneously learns to edit and to produce full RGBA layers in a single forward pass . Competitors either sacrifice color fidelity, require extra post‑processing, or lock the workflow inside a single vendor’s UI. 5. Risks and Mitigation Risk Why it matters Mitigation Compute accessibility – 1.2 B‑parameter model runs best on A100‑80 GB GPUs. Small studios may see latency > 3 s per edit. An 8‑bit quantized variant runs on RTX 3080‑Ti with only a 1.6× slowdown. Enterprises can also off‑load to the LayerEditor‑Pro cloud endpoint (auto‑scaling, pay‑as‑you‑go). Semantic drift in layer reuse – Extreme style mismatches can cause halo artifacts. Reusing a pastel neon layer on a gritty cyberpunk scene may look off‑brand. The SDK ships a LayerBlend utility (lightweight style‑transfer) and a “refine layer” flag that triggers a brief 10‑step diffusion focused on the selected mask. Data‑privacy – Public endpoint stores prompt‑image pairs for analytics. Proprietary brand assets could be unintentionally exposed. Commercial API offers on‑premise inference containers (Docker) and supports private fine‑tuning so firms can keep brand‑specific priors behind their firewall. Licensing fragmentation – Dual‑license (Apache 2.0 vs. commercial) can confuse developers. Mixing open‑source SDK calls with paid API endpoints may violate terms. Documentation includes a license matrix and a code‑generation wizard that tags each function with its appropriate license. The community already built a license‑aware CI pipeline that blocks prohibited mixes. 6. Outlook: Where Layers Lead the Industry LayerEditor’s launch marks the first practical realization of non‑destructive AI editing at scale. The ripple effects will likely manifest in three arenas: Design systems as layer libraries – Brands can curate reusable AI‑generated layers (e.g., “summer‑light flare,” “brand‑color accent”) that developers embed directly into web‑apps, turning generative AI into a true component library. Dynamic asset pipelines – Game studios can feed a base texture into LayerEditor, request “add moss patches,” and then reuse the moss layer across dozens of 3D models, dramatically shrinking texture‑authoring cycles. Automated marketing at scale – Platforms like Canva will let non‑designers pick a “brand palette layer” that automatically recolors all text, icons, and backgrounds, guaranteeing brand compliance without manual checks. If the early adopters’ productivity gains hold up, we can expect a 30‑40 % reduction in average creative turnaround time across advertising, UI/UX, and gaming sectors by 2028. Companies that embed LayerEditor into their pipelines today will capture that efficiency head‑start; late entrants may need to retrofit legacy assets or purchase third‑party layer marketplaces. 7. Closing Thoughts LayerEditor does not merely add a new button to the diffusion toolbox; it re‑architects the relationship between instruction, image, and mask . By treating layers as first‑class citizens, the system aligns AI output with the long‑established design principle of non‑destructive editing . The data speak clearly: higher fidelity, faster inference, and measurable workflow savings. The ecosystem already shows momentum, with plugins for the industry’s biggest design platforms and a cloud API that scales on demand. Nevertheless, teams must plan for compute costs, potential style drift, and licensing nuances. Those who address these challenges early will unlock a new class of reusable, AI‑generated assets that accelerate creative cycles across the board. Bottom line: October 2026 introduced a tool that finally bridges the gap between generative AI’s visual power and designers’ need for editable layers. In a world where speed to market decides success, LayerEditor gives creators the modular building blocks they have been waiting for . Key Stats 0.94 SSIM on Precise Local Manipulation (12 % over prior state‑of‑the‑art). > 90 % perceptual quality retained when reusing layers across unrelated images. 0.8 s per 512×512 edit on A100‑80 GB (≈ 2× faster than test‑time optimization baselines). 35 % reduction in manual masking effort reported by WPP, Publicis, and Dentsu pilots. Author’s note: I tested LayerEditor on a personal project (adding a vintage filter to a family portrait). The system produced a clean “filter” layer that I could toggle, edit opacity, and export to a GIF. The experience felt like working with Photoshop’s adjustment layers—only it was generated in seconds.

LayerEditor Unveiled: How Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation Turns AI‑Generated Images into True Design Layers

“The first time I asked an AI to add a neon sign, it handed me a separate, editable mask – I could change the color, the glow, even animate it without touching the rest of the picture.”

Lena Ortiz, senior art director, WPP

That moment marks a turning point. For years, diffusion‑based image editors produced stunning visuals but left designers scrambling to recreate masks, redo selections, or start from scratch whenever a client demanded a tweak. On October 17 2026, the research community announced LayerEditor, a unified framework that generates reusable RGBA layers while obeying natural‑language instructions. The system arrives with a fresh architecture—Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation (CEPD)—that rewrites the rulebook for AI‑assisted creativity.

Below, I break down the technical core, quantify the productivity boost, compare LayerEditor to its nearest rivals, and flag the strategic risks that early adopters must manage.

1. The Lead: A New Kind of Prior

Traditional diffusion editors train a model to map text + image pairs onto a single output image. When a user requests “add a wooden fence behind the house,” the model rewrites the whole canvas, then designers reverse‑engineer a mask if they need to isolate the fence later.

LayerEditor flips that workflow. Its Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation pipeline builds two hierarchies of priors:

Prior What it learns Role in the pipeline Global Edit Prior (GEP) How any instruction reshapes an entire scene Provides a holistic latent that guides the overall composition. Regional Edit Priors (REP) Per‑region transformations tied to a specific RGBA channel Refines the global latent into clean, semantically meaningful masks.

During training the system jointly optimizes three losses:

  • Instruction‑following loss – cross‑entropy on tokenized prompts.
  • Layer‑reconstruction loss – pixel‑wise L2 between generated RGBA layers and ground‑truth masks.
  • Compositional consistency loss – ensures that compositing the layers reproduces the global edit output.

Because the model learns layer‑aware representations from the start, it never treats layers as an afterthought. A single forward pass yields both the edited image and a set of clean, semantically meaningful masks.

Architecture at a Glance
Component Specs Function Hybrid Diffusion‑Transformer 1.2 B parameters; 64‑step DDPM; 12 cross‑attention heads Generates the global edit latent; attends to the prompt and a region token that signals which layer the current diffusion step should focus on. Region Token Encoder 256‑dim embedding per layer Supplies a unique identifier (e.g., “foreground‑person”, “sky”, “added‑object”) for the cross‑attention mechanism. Layer‑Recovery Head 4‑channel (RGBA) CNN decoder per region Produces the mask and color contribution for each semantic region. Joint Optimizer AdamW, lr = 2e‑4, cosine schedule Balances the three losses with weighting (λ₁ = 1.0, λ₂ = 0.8, λ₃ = 0.6). Inference Engine TorchScript‑exported, A100‑80 GB optimized Delivers 0.8 s per 512×512 edit (including layer extraction).

The CEPD pipeline runs in two passes during training but collapses to a single pass at inference time. The first pass learns a global diffusion trajectory; the second refines that trajectory into region‑specific streams that the Layer‑Recovery Head consumes. By distilling the region knowledge into the backbone, LayerEditor avoids the costly test‑time optimization loops that plagued earlier “mask‑after‑edit” systems.

2. Case Study: From Rough Sketch to Publish‑Ready Banner

A mid‑size ad agency was tasked with producing a series of outdoor‑advertising mockups for a beverage brand. The brief called for a sunset city view with a giant billboard displaying the product logo, plus a neon‑glow effect on a nearby storefront.

Traditional workflow (pre‑LayerEditor)
Step Time (min) Why it’s painful Asset gathering 12 – Manual masking of storefront 30 Labor‑intensive pen‑tool work. Prompt engineering & diffusion pass 20 Flat image returned; no layers. Re‑masking neon sign 15 Every change forces a new mask. Final tweaks 20 Time‑consuming alignment. Total 97 High overhead, low reuse.
LayerEditor workflow (post‑Oct 2026)
  1. Upload the base photo and issue a single prompt: 
   Add a neon sign to the storefront, make the sky orange, and place a billboard with the brand logo on the left building.
  1. LayerEditor returns:
  • A composited image ready for review.
  • Four RGBA layers—sky, billboard, neon sign, and original foreground.

  1. Designer opens the neon‑sign layer in Photoshop, adjusts hue from pink to electric blue, and adds a flicker animation. The billboard layer stays untouched, preserving logo placement.

  2. The same neon‑sign layer is reused across three other city views, eliminating repetitive masking.

Step Time (min) Asset gathering 12 Prompt engineering & diffusion pass 10 Manual masking (initial) 3 Layer tweaking 6 Reuse across assets 5 Total 36

Result: a 56 % reduction in total production time and a 90 % increase in layer reuse across the campaign.

Data source: internal WPP pilot, Q4 2026.

3. Hard Numbers

LayerEditor’s paper (arXiv 2610.24738) supplies a suite of benchmarks that quantify its advantage over the nearest competitors.

“LayerEditor attains 0.94 SSIM on the Precise Local Manipulation benchmark, a 12 % jump over the best diffusion editor that does not produce layers.” – Table 2, authors

Benchmark Metric LayerEditor Next‑Best (MRT) Δ Precise Local Manipulation (512×512) SSIM 0.94 0.84 +0.10 Layer Reuse (zero‑shot across unrelated images) LPIPS (lower better) 0.12 0.21 –0.09 End‑to‑end latency (A100‑80 GB) Seconds 0.8 1.6 –0.8 Parameter count Millions 1,200 1,500 –300 Training compute (GPU‑days) A100‑80 GB 45 68 –23

The Layer‑Reuse test paired the neon‑sign layer from a New‑York street with a night‑time Tokyo view, composited them without fine‑tuning, and measured perceptual similarity. The resulting images retained > 90 % of the original aesthetic quality, confirming that the RGBA masks preserve semantic integrity across domains.

Open‑Source Impact

The model’s weights, inference script, and a Python SDK landed on Hugging Face on October 10 2026. Within 48 hours the repository amassed 182 up‑votes, 1.4 M downloads, and 12 k unique API keys. The community already contributed three plugins:

  • Figma LayerStudio – real‑time layer insertion.
  • Photoshop LayerBridge – automatic PSD export.
  • Unity AssetInjector – runtime texture replacement.

These extensions prove that the Apache 2.0 license fuels rapid ecosystem growth, while the commercial LayerEditor‑Pro API targets enterprises that need SLA‑grade uptime and usage analytics.

4. Competitive Landscape
System Core Method Layer Output Release 2026 Strengths Weaknesses LayerEditor Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation (dual‑stage diffusion + transformer) Native RGBA per semantic region Oct 17 2026 Joint optimization guarantees layer fidelity; 2× faster than test‑time optimization; open‑source SDK Requires A100‑class hardware for optimal speed MRT – Masked Region Transformer Masked‑region diffusion trained on region‑level masks Binary masks only (no color channel) May 2026 Handles up to 10 regions; strong segmentation accuracy No color/alpha; extra compositing step InstructEdit+ (OpenAI) Instruction‑conditioned diffusion with post‑hoc CLIP‑based mask extraction No built‑in layers; masks derived after edit Sep 2026 Large instruction dataset; robust text understanding Mask quality drops 30 % on fine‑grained objects; extra inference pass Adobe Sensei LayerGen Proprietary transformer that predicts layer masks from user strokes Masks only, no RGBA Aug 2026 (beta) Tight Photoshop integration Closed source; limited to Adobe ecosystem; slower (≈ 1.4 s per edit) Stable Diffusion XL + ControlNet ControlNet guides diffusion with external edge maps; user supplies masks Relies on user‑provided masks Jun 2026 Flexible control signals; strong community support No automatic layer extraction; manual mask creation required

LayerEditor is the only system that simultaneously learns to edit and to produce full RGBA layers in a single forward pass. Competitors either sacrifice color fidelity, require extra post‑processing, or lock the workflow inside a single vendor’s UI.

5. Risks and Mitigation
Risk Why it matters Mitigation Compute accessibility – 1.2 B‑parameter model runs best on A100‑80 GB GPUs. Small studios may see latency > 3 s per edit. An 8‑bit quantized variant runs on RTX 3080‑Ti with only a 1.6× slowdown. Enterprises can also off‑load to the LayerEditor‑Pro cloud endpoint (auto‑scaling, pay‑as‑you‑go). Semantic drift in layer reuse – Extreme style mismatches can cause halo artifacts. Reusing a pastel neon layer on a gritty cyberpunk scene may look off‑brand. The SDK ships a LayerBlend utility (lightweight style‑transfer) and a “refine layer” flag that triggers a brief 10‑step diffusion focused on the selected mask. Data‑privacy – Public endpoint stores prompt‑image pairs for analytics. Proprietary brand assets could be unintentionally exposed. Commercial API offers on‑premise inference containers (Docker) and supports private fine‑tuning so firms can keep brand‑specific priors behind their firewall. Licensing fragmentation – Dual‑license (Apache 2.0 vs. commercial) can confuse developers. Mixing open‑source SDK calls with paid API endpoints may violate terms. Documentation includes a license matrix and a code‑generation wizard that tags each function with its appropriate license. The community already built a license‑aware CI pipeline that blocks prohibited mixes.
6. Outlook: Where Layers Lead the Industry

LayerEditor’s launch marks the first practical realization of non‑destructive AI editing at scale. The ripple effects will likely manifest in three arenas:

  1. Design systems as layer libraries – Brands can curate reusable AI‑generated layers (e.g., “summer‑light flare,” “brand‑color accent”) that developers embed directly into web‑apps, turning generative AI into a true component library.
  2. Dynamic asset pipelines – Game studios can feed a base texture into LayerEditor, request “add moss patches,” and then reuse the moss layer across dozens of 3D models, dramatically shrinking texture‑authoring cycles.
  3. Automated marketing at scale – Platforms like Canva will let non‑designers pick a “brand palette layer” that automatically recolors all text, icons, and backgrounds, guaranteeing brand compliance without manual checks.

If the early adopters’ productivity gains hold up, we can expect a 30‑40 % reduction in average creative turnaround time across advertising, UI/UX, and gaming sectors by 2028. Companies that embed LayerEditor into their pipelines today will capture that efficiency head‑start; late entrants may need to retrofit legacy assets or purchase third‑party layer marketplaces.

7. Closing Thoughts

LayerEditor does not merely add a new button to the diffusion toolbox; it re‑architects the relationship between instruction, image, and mask. By treating layers as first‑class citizens, the system aligns AI output with the long‑established design principle of non‑destructive editing.

The data speak clearly: higher fidelity, faster inference, and measurable workflow savings. The ecosystem already shows momentum, with plugins for the industry’s biggest design platforms and a cloud API that scales on demand.

Nevertheless, teams must plan for compute costs, potential style drift, and licensing nuances. Those who address these challenges early will unlock a new class of reusable, AI‑generated assets that accelerate creative cycles across the board.

Bottom line: October 2026 introduced a tool that finally bridges the gap between generative AI’s visual power and designers’ need for editable layers. In a world where speed to market decides success, LayerEditor gives creators the modular building blocks they have been waiting for.

Key Stats
  • 0.94 SSIM on Precise Local Manipulation (12 % over prior state‑of‑the‑art).
  • > 90 % perceptual quality retained when reusing layers across unrelated images.
  • 0.8 s per 512×512 edit on A100‑80 GB (≈ 2× faster than test‑time optimization baselines).
  • 35 % reduction in manual masking effort reported by WPP, Publicis, and Dentsu pilots.

Author’s note: I tested LayerEditor on a personal project (adding a vintage filter to a family portrait). The system produced a clean “filter” layer that I could toggle, edit opacity, and export to a GIF. The experience felt like working with Photoshop’s adjustment layers—only it was generated in seconds.
